That this House commends the Government of Manitoba for its positive policies of job creation which have produced the lowest unemployment level in Canada, and calls upon the Government to adopt a similar course of economic expansion rather than the discredited policies of tax increases and spending cuts which it has pursued to date and which are largely responsible for the latest unemployment statistics, which show an alarming increase of 167,000 unemployed between December, 1984 and January, 1985.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to lead off for the New Democratic Party on its Opposition Day motion. In a sense, the motion identifies the number one issue which faces the country-unemployment.
If we look around at a variety of models, there are some areas of the world and, indeed, some areas of Canada that provide us with some guidance as to what the present federal Government ought to be using as it develops its plans for the Budget and the ways and means it will use to get the economy of Canada back on track.
As a youngster I was a fan of Robert Louis Stevenson. He wrote a book entitled The Wreckers. The fundamental theme in that book was that a group of rather unscrupulous people on a South Pacific island set up large bonfires in the evenings on certain parts of the beach. Those bonfires were to act as beacons to ships which were sailing past and to indicate to them that those were safe areas in which to anchor. However, there were hidden shoals and when the large ships sailed in they were shipwrecked. Then the unscrupulous island people would plunder the contents of the ships, and as a result people would lose their lives.
I was reminded of that story when thinking about the nature of this debate. The federal Government is saying: "Follow us". The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) is saying: "Have faith in us. Just give us time, because we are providing guidance".
Human wreckage has resulted from that policy and that kind of direction. I do not have to go any further than my own constituency. Kamloops has an official unemployment rate of 20.3 per cent. In real terms, that means there are over 10,000
people in that region who are officially collecting unemployment insurance, over 5,500 people on welfare, and hundreds of others who do not qualify for unemployment insurance or welfare support. There are small-business people who do not qualify and fall through the social security net. There are 2,500 young people under the age of 25 who are jobless in that community. The Minister tells them not to worry because Canada Works will provide jobs. There are more than 15,000 who are unemployed and Canada Works may provide 200 jobs in the next few months. The Minister of Employment and Immigration tells us to have faith in the Government and to be patient because the private sector in Kamloops will provide thousands of jobs in the next little while.
Last weekend I was in my constituency and met with three business groups. The groups, which speak for small and medium-sized businesses, said that they were literally clinging to survival and that they were not thinking about expansion. They told me that the best scenario which could happen was that they would not go bankrupt. I also met with representatives of the ministerial association, pastors from a number of churches in the greater Kamloops area. They said that if things did not change dramatically over the next few months there would be violence, civil disobedience and bloodshed in the streets. That was told to me by pastors who are the heads of their congregations. These are people who have not only a compassion but an understanding of the realities on the main streets of Kamloops.
[DOT] (mo)
I see Hon. Members opposite laughing at that proposal. The heads of churches say that there will in fact be blood running and violence in these communities because of the economic policies being pursued by Governments in this country. Those are not my views necessarily. I am simply reflecting the views of the religious leaders in my community.
I received a letter this morning from a young man who has worked for the last 12 years but who lost his job a few months ago. He ran out of his unemployment insurance benefits. A few weeks ago he went down to the welfare office to apply for a subsidy and was told that they could not give him one at the time because his wife was working and earning $525 a month. This couple's rent for a very modest apartment is $375. They have just received a bill from B.C. Hydro for a two-month period in the amount of $148. That leaves them $2, Mr. Speaker, to live on for the month. That $2 will have to pay for their food and all the other incidentals which life demands.
This young husband is a proud man and he sees today no hope. He is told by Government services that he does not qualify for a subsidy but if he comes back in two or three

months it might be able to find a $60 a month supplement for him. Some of us in this House should try living on $2 a month. What this means, of course, is that this proud individual will now have to go downtown and get in line at the food bank. If he is lucky he will get a hamper of food after standing in line for an hour or so because inevitably at the end of the day the food supply runs out and has to be replenished. This is a reality now in one of the richest parts of Canada traditionally. This is a reality in a province which is identified as a "have" province. It is recognized as a very prosperous province generally, but the Province of British Columbia, Mr. Speaker, is on its knees. It is an economic basket case.
For a moment, Mr. Speaker, I would like to turn our attention away from that part of Canada. We found out a few days ago that unemployment has soared, increasing more in one month than it has in any single month over the last five years. The increase in the number of people who are unemployed in Canada over the last month is the equivalent of the population of cities like Sudbury, Saskatoon, Chicoutimi, Oshawa, St. John's. In other words, the size of the entire population of a city was added to the unemployment rolls in one single month. But the Government still says "Be patient, folks; relax. We are consulting with various groups and so on. We will be bringing in a Budget some time in April or May". The Budget will take effect in terms of its policy in the fall or next winter some time, but the Government says "Just relax".
I suspect that the people of Canada are not prepared to relax much longer. There are one and a half million people in this country who are unemployed and that number is growing. That means one and a half million people are not playing their rightful role in Canadian society of building the Canadian economy. There are fewer houses under construction, fewer roads being built, fewer trees being planted and fewer consumer goods being produced, all because one and a half million people are idle.
On top of that there is the cost of nearly $ 1 billion a month for unemployment insurance benefits from the federal Government, plus hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars in welfare payments out of the federal Government's treasury in terms of transfer payments. We cannot afford these high levels of unemployment in the country, Mr. Speaker, because of what it does to the productive capacity in Canada and what it costs Canadians.
What has been the argument and the proposals of our Governments, Mr. Speaker? I believe we could distil the alternatives down to two. There is one school of thought which thinks the solution to unemployment is to unshackle the market-place; free enterprise, some would say. To these people, government bureaucracies are the root of all evil. If we reduce government, the private sector will enthusiastically come to life, spring into action and develop, expand and create those jobs, is the explanation we hear from the Conservatives.
John Kenneth Galbraith summed it up I think quite nicely when he said that these are the folks who believe that the rich
are not working because they have too little money and the poor are not working because they have too much money.
These people want to take us back to an earlier time in the past when they believed government was less intrusive in the lives of individuals. How are they prepared to do that? They want to reduce the size of government. Their very first priority is to reduce expenditures on social programs and slash the deficit no matter what the consequences. This is what we have seen in the Province of British Columbia. This is the reality of the world of Bill Bennett.
In his statement on November 8 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) outlined the Government's priorities. At the top of the list was not job creation or economic development; at the top of the list was deficit reduction. The Minister's statements on November 8 sounded strangely similar to those statements of the Premier of British Columbia in his last two budgets.
Let me give a couple of examples. On November 8 the Minister of Finance said that controlling the deficit must be our priority for this year and each year of the Government's mandate. The B.C. budget of 1973 said that the Government's decision is clear-"We shall restrain expenditure and reduce the size of government". Again on November 8 the federal Minister of Finance said he believes that deficit reduction is the key to rebuilding confidence. The B.C. budget of 1983 said that the budget provides what is needed to contain the size and burden of government so the private sector, our major resource companies and all businesses large and small, will have the climate needed to ensure that our fragile recovery gains momentum.
Let us look at what happened in British Columbia. In 1983 they looked into the future and made some projections, as did the federal Minister of Finance. In B.C. they said that real provincial growth will occur in the 6 per cent range. Capital investment will increase by 15 per cent in 1984 and employment growth will increase nearly 4 per cent. That is what they thought was going to happen. That is what they wished was going to happen. It is a Peter Pan approach to economics; if you really believe it is going to happen, it will happen.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it did not happen. Real provincial growth was less than 1 per cent. In other words, it decreased. There was no economic growth in British Columbia. Capital investment fell by 5 per cent rather than increasing by 15 per cent. Employment growth fell. In other words, unemployment is increasing at a staggering rate month after month after month. What they projected simply did not occur.
While it is not surprising that opposition Members, particularly New Democrats from British Columbia, would have a rather jaundiced view of what has happened, we are not the only ones. I can quote the president of the Chartered Accountants' Association of British Columbia. On October 19, 1984 he said that B.C. is heading for hell in a hand-basket this winter. He said many of his members are telling their clients to flee British Columbia. In other words, if you are looking for opportunity, for growth and development, for investment
February 12, 1985

opportunities, do not stay in British Columbia, go east to Manitoba.
That is what Michael Walker, the chief economist for the Fraser Institute, had to say to young people. They asked him what he would suggest they do in British Columbia and he said the best news he had for young people in British Columbia is not the old "Go west, young man"; it is "Go east, young man". He meant go east to Manitoba.
How do you know that?

That is where the jobs are. That is where the in-migration is taking place. There is none to British Columbia, believe me.
The Royal Bank of Canada came out with a report in Manitoba, 1984, which said that B.C.'s problems include severe government restraint measures, persistent labour disputes, depressed consumer and business confidence. The president of the Business Council of British Columbia said the economy has not recovered, it has not turned around, and that is what we were all led to believe.
One can go on and on, Mr. Speaker, and list spokesperson after spokesperson from economic and financial agencies, respected analysts in their field. When they are honest they all say that the future of British Columbia under the restraint policy and conservative ideology of the Social Credit Government is very depressing. Most of the money now raised on the Vancouver Stock Exchange is for investment outside of British Columbia. That says something about how the investors of British Columbia feel about the future of their province.
It would be useful to turn to another alternative now. I indicated that one alternative was this almost religious zeal which sees the unfettered market-place as the opportunity for our economic future. Another alternative is that which we see in the Province of Manitoba. Jobs are the first priority of the Manitoba Government. Its first priority is to get the people of Manitoba working in meaningful, long-term jobs. The Government of Manitoba assumes that unemployment erodes economic growth and investor and consumer confidence. It assumes that if people have jobs they can sustain the necessary economic activity and provide the consumer demand which is the real trigger to business confidence and investment.
The Conservatives feel it is necessary to bribe people to behave in certain economic ways. They want to lure and entice business to expand. They want to provide tax incentives. Business does not need to be bribed or to have incentives provided for it. If there is a market-place and a consuming public, businesses will expand. They will not expand if there is no one to purchase their goods and services. Any government which believes it works the other way around is sorely mistaken.
The Minister of Finance in the Province of Manitoba, Mr. Schroeder, has said: "It is vitally important that the provincial Government stimulus takes place now to protect our basic

strengths and enhance our ability to promote the advancement of economic recovery when it comes". In December of 1982 he said: "Efforts to reduce deficits through large-scale tax increases or expenditure cuts will only aggravate current economic problems". Manitoba has taken some very concrete action which has reduced the level of unemployment in that province. The Province of Manitoba now has the lowest unemployment level in Canada. Manitoba is a have-not province. It is not usually identified as a prosperous province. The Government of Manitoba meant it when it said that job creation and development was its number one priority.
The Government of Manitoba took action on a variety of fronts. In 1983 it put together a jobs fund. It allocated $200 million for the creation of jobs. In 1983 alone it created 21,000 jobs. In the first half of 1984 it created 10,000 jobs. If the national Government provided an equal ratio of job creation stimulus it would be spending $5 billion on getting people back to work. However, the federal Government would rather spend $12 billion on UIC payments or hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars on welfare. It would much rather do as it did last month and spend $300 million buying up Canadian dollars. Week after week the Government spends hundreds of millions of dollars to buy its own dollars in order artificially to prop up the value of the Canadian dollar because Mr. Bouey has a passionate and committed position to maintain the dollar at 75 cents U.S. Therefore we will spend $300 million this month and perhaps another $200 million next month. Do I hear a single Conservative Member state in the House that that notion is wrong and should not be the way to spend taxpayers' money in this country? There is never a word from them.
Let me give some examples of programs that are funded under this jobs fund in the Province of Manitoba. There is the development of a technology resource centre in which major computer companies participated.
I see that my time is almost up.

The Conservatives say "good" because it must be very hard on them when I point out that Manitoba is the one province in Canada where business investment is the highest per capita and where there is a migration of people into that province because that is where the opportunities exist in western Canada. Unemployment is the lowest in that province which just happens to have a New Democratic Party Government. Those are the facts.
In conclusion, if the Government is really committed to its election campaign that jobs was its number one priority, it can look at models on which to base its programs. It can look at the conservative Government in the Province of British Columbia which is ruining that economy, or at the Province of Manitoba that has developed one of the stronger economies in the country. Jobs are in fact being created on a daily basis. People are migrating there and government investment, con-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the Hon. Member's speech. I have also read the motion. Given the Hon. Member's interest in the House and the fact that he has been here since 1980, does he recall there ever being an Opposition motion presented which was so subservient to the interests of a political party in a province?

Mr. Speaker, I think I understand the question. Let me preface my remarks by saying that not only have I been here for five years, but I have been an observer of the House of Commons for many more years. I have also been a concerned Canadian for 43 years. I believe we are at the most critical point in the future of our country. I do not believe there has been a Budget presented in the last three or four decades that has been more important than the upcoming Budget.
As a Member of Parliament from British Columbia, 1 see a particular political ideology at work in the economy. We can quote many people besides opposition politicians who describe that approach as being disastrous, one that simply leads to more unemployment and less confidence. It is a plan that results in a loss of hope for the future by older and younger Canadians in that province.
Last night I met with five businessmen from Vancouver. They are leaders in that economy and I asked them about their opinion of the economy for the next six months. They said that they saw absolutely no hope for the next six months and only wishful thinking after that.
That is why we felt it is important at this point, when we know that the Government is serious about finding a proper solution to get the economy of Canada back on track, to look to other models. The Government could look to Australia or Great Britain, but we felt that rather than looking at the international community it could look to Canada where there are two models to draw upon for information. That is why we selected the one real success story in Canada today as a model. The model just happens to be headed by a New Democratic Party Government. I suspect if it were headed by some other government, we would still identify Manitoba as an appropriate province.
Let us look at the successes, Mr. Speaker. Why do we look at failures for a model? This tells us a little bit about the Conservatives. They look around and say: "Listen, the economy of Great Britain is falling on its face, the economy of British Columbia is falling on its face; let us use these two
areas as our models". We say let us use other countries as our models. Let us use as a model what is going on in Australia, where the unemployment rate is 8 per cent today. Perhaps we should look at Sweden or Norway where the unemployment rate is 3 per cent today. Let us look at West Germany where interest rates today are 5.5 per cent.
Many people have been caught up with the Tory rhetoric that this is it, that this is the reality, that there is no alternative. Our responsibility as a concerned and effective Opposition is to say there are other alternatives. The Province of Manitoba is one of those other alternatives.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the Hon. Member's concern about the creation of jobs and the availability of jobs that comes through Canada's capacity to compete in the great markets of the Department of Defence of the United States or in other markets covering anything from toothpicks to mattresses to computers to military equipment, and if it offsets our gain, would the Hon. Member support the creation of additional jobs in his riding or in the Province of British Columbia where Canadian businessmen can compete? Does the Hon. Member encourage and support that kind of activity?

Mr. Speaker, I speak for my Party when I say that the kind of jobs and the kind of economic enterprise that we would like to see support for today is not necessarily the kind of enterprise that is associated with the build-up of the American arms industry.
The mayors of Canada came together and said: "You, the Government of Canada, we have billions and billions of needed urban infrastructure that must be built". It is not a question of should be built; it has to be built. I am talking about sewage treatment, water treatment facilities, senior citizens' housing, other kinds of social housing, roads, bridges. In other words, things that will be with us for decades and perhaps generations. How long does a tank last? How long does a bullet last? How long does any military technology last? It might be valid for a few weeks, a few months, at best a few years.
We are concerned that it is time now to develop the necessary supports to develop the processing, the secondary industry, the tertiary industry and the quaternary industry of this country. I do not see the present Government doing that. I see the present Government getting off on a tangent and, if you like, maintaining the status quo, saying to the large corporations: "We are going to rely on you to expand the economy". I hear a brilliant statement coming from a Conservative opposite. That is the kind of positive criticism that we can expect.

I am suggesting that if we are going to develop the economy of Canada, we know what can be done within Canada. We know we have the resources within Canada to accomplish that; we have the will of the people, the expertise and the capital.
We in the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker, have faith in the people of Canada. We do not have to look outside for alternatives. We do not have to look outside for our investment money. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The Hon. Member mentioned particularly a lot of interest in Manitoba. Is the Hon. Member recommending to the Government of Mr. Pawley that the contracts with Bristol-Myers and other major employers in that area should be cancelled, or should they be expanded when there is opportunity to expand? Will the Hon. Member support that expansion and those additional jobs, or does the Hon. Member want to do away with the 30,000 jobs in Canada involved with these industries? Does the Hon. Member support that industry or does he not?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the point the Hon. Member is making. I have two responses for him. One, I am not going to suggest what any provincial Government should or should not do. Provincial Governments are quite capable of deciding on their own. I am suggesting some alternatives for our national Government.
I think it is appropriate, if we want to get a return on our investment of federal dollars, that we develop our educational system and our manufacturing industries. That is where the greatest return is. Take a look at our resource industries. Why do we not start processing some of those resources? In other words, we should do something new. We should initiate something new in terms of economic development. That is what the Government is elected to do. It was elected on a change of policy. It was not elected to perpetuate the same policy to which the Liberals introduced us for many, many years.

speechtext: Does anyone wish to speak on debate?
Mr. Speaker, since the Party that is responsible for our current crisis chooses not to speak on the issue, I will be happy to speak on it.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker I take part in this debate with considerable pride. I have roots in Manitoba through a great uncle who homesteaded there during a period when times were really tough in western Canada and it took a great sense of challenge and adventure to live there. I am very proud of the people in my family who are in Carman, Manitoba, and who have been proud supporters of my political Party and our political concepts.
I am pleased to take part in this debate because my hon. friend started off with a reference to two things that are of interest to me. One was to ships and harbours and I note that Manitoba is one of our provinces fronting on the ocean. I would also like to quote for my hon. friend his favourite author, Robert Louis Stevenson:
You cannot run away from a weakness; you must some time fight it out or perish; and if that be so, why not now ... ?
Mankind was never so happily inspired as when it made a cathedral.
We are attempting to make this country once again a cathedral.
I am also pleased to take part in this debate because it raises some important economic and fiscal issues that we on this side of the House have been attempting to debate in an intelligent way. It is certainly nice to see members of the Opposition accepting our invitation to join in the national debate on the directions for change set up by this Government. It provides an opportunity to discuss issues in what I hope will be a rational and constructive way. Toward that end I will try and overlook the possibility that the motion is really more concerned with politics than it is with economics, or even with Robert Louis Stevenson.
I am pleased to commend any provincial government that puts forward positive policies for economic growth and job creation. To the extent that the Manitoba Government has done that, I say "well done" and I hope that Government keeps it up.
Since the motion cites Manitoba as a model, I want to take a moment to look at the facts of the case. First, the employment situation. Manitoba's unemployment rate at 8.5 per cent in January was equal to that of Saskatchewan as the lowest among the provinces, significantly below the national average of 11.2 per cent. Perhaps it was just an oversight that the

drafters of the motion forgot to include Saskatchewan in the commendation. In any case I hope the omission has nothing to do with the fact that there is, after all, a Progressive Conservative Government in the Province of Saskatchewan.

Let us now look at the percentage increase in employment in Manitoba since the end of the recession. At 6.3 per cent, the increase is slightly above the national average of 6.1 per cent but below the range of 8 per cent or higher in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Quebec and Ontario. Manitoba's loss of jobs during the recession at 4.3 per cent was below the national average of 5.2 per cent. In other words, its employment situation has been more stable but has shown less growth.
Since September when the Government took office, 64,000 jobs have been created in Canada and the unemployment rate has dropped. The rate of job creation in the past four months has been 1,200 per cent faster than in the same period a year earlier. I might also note, according to some recent information, that Manitoba's economic growth rate for this year is forecast at about the national average.
It is clear that attempts to draw sweeping conclusions about the success or otherwise of any given set of economic policies over relatively short periods are unconvincing, to put it mildly. They could be dismissed as harmless exercises if they did not illustrate, as the motion before the House clearly does, the continuing tendency to look for simplistic alternatives to the hard economic and fiscal challenges which are facing the nation. The Throne Speech, the economic statement, the First Ministers' conference and the national summit are all part of the renewal of the Canadian economy. These events and the consultation process are the essence of the consensus building necessary for a bright and prosperous future. We have made the renewal of the Canadian economy the top priority, with economic growth, economic opportunities and jobs our main concern.
It is simplistic, not to mention mischievous, to attribute the employment creation of provinces to provincial government policies while at the same time blaming the federal Government generally for unemployment across the country. That same federal Government's tax revenues in Manitoba have been considerably exceeded by federal spending in the province, spending in the form of federal employee wages, family allowances, unemployment insurance, old age pensions and federal-provincial transfers such as equalization, hospital insurance, medicare, post-secondary education and social assistance under the Canada Assistance Plan.
The federal Government has demonstrated its support for the well-being of Canadians. We remain fundamentally committed to that well-being, no matter where those Canadians may live in this great land. That is why the Government has come forward with the kinds of policies needed to renew the capacity of the economy of all Canada to grow and create lasting new jobs. I want to emphasize for the benefit of Hon. Members across the way the word "lasting", because it is
crucial to the kind of economic process which the Government wants to build.
If I may be allowed one last look at the Manitoba situation-and this was the idea of Hon. Members across the way-we could indeed find evidence of significant public spending for job-creation purposes. About $200 million annually has been funnelled through the Manitoba jobs fund to small and medium-sized businesses in 1983-84, although I note that some economists have argued that the program does not represent new initiatives but a repackaging of existing programs. In any case, the new program has generated jobs lasting about 13 weeks on average.
As much as programs of this nature are needed, the hard fact remains that the real need is long-term jobs. Strong concern has been expressed in Manitoba over the lack of emphasis on private sector investment which leads to those opportunities. Also, the Manitoba budget last year indicated such a shift in its Government's approach to seeking longer term job opportunities.
We welcome the efforts of Governments in every province to deal with both short and long-term economic needs. We particularly welcome evidence and other Governments increasingly recognize the need for getting at the causes of economic weakness rather than merely suppressing the symptoms with more and more borrowed money. The fiscal situation of the Government of Canada, record high deficits and rapidly rising accumulated debt brought to us courtesy of the Liberal Party, is a legacy of just that kind of philosophy. This is why I fail to understand why the Liberal Party has chosen not to speak on this topic. It was a Government so fixated on treating the economic symptoms that its policies became part of the disease; it spent money as if there were no tomorrow. It was right but only in terms of its own political prospects. Unfortunately it bequeathed a lot of very expensive tomorrows for all Canadians.
We are trying to eliminate the cause of our economic weakness through an attack on the growing mountain of national debt. This is part of our comprehensive program to build a healthy and expanding economy which will create jobs and economic opportunity. Other speakers will have more time to address the fiscal situation which faces the Government. I will only say that we are at a point where the use of the kind of conventional fiscal stimulus suggested by the motion before the House would not be expansionary for the economy in any but the most fleeting and ephemeral senses. The damage to confidence would take its toll on private sector investment, and the Government's future fiscal capacity to assist in economic growth would be further eroded. In short, we cannot go on this way.
I remind Hon. Members opposite of an important maxim: we cannot cross a river in two strides. It takes time and many steps to brook a river to get us where we want to go. We have already started to take strides in the right direction. Putting the Government's fiscal house in order is therefore a crucial element in the agenda for economic renewal which the Government has placed before the country and before the
February 12, 1985

House-first, for debate here and consultation with the country, and then for action.
Contrary to the motion before the House, the Government has begun the task of restraining government expenditures in a manner entirely compatible with the continued growth of the economy and the creation of new jobs. The notion of the props being pulled out from under the economy by government restraint is totally ludicrous. In fact, even after the effect of expenditure reductions and other measures brought forward in November, the projected deficit in the next fiscal year will represent an additional stimulus of some $7 billion over and above what the previous Government had projected. If we take the motion at its face value, it is telling us that the prospect of this extra $7 billion and all the higher than expected deficits of recent years are doing little or nothing to help the economy produce the real jobs which Canadians need. That is precisely the problem which the Government is addressing by facing the deficit and the debt head on. We want to solve the problem before it becomes a crisis.
In its agenda for action the Government has set out to redefine its role so that it can provide an effective framework for the growth and job creation we need. That means removing the obstacles to change and innovation to enable the private sector to keep up with competition from around the world. We intend to foster the necessary increases in investment in a climate favourable to the birth and growth of new enterprise. We will achieve those goals in a manner which is fair and open and with the basic sense of compassion and tolerance which are very much a part of the Canadian fabric and very much a part of this Party's record. However, government alone cannot bring about economic renewal. We have put forward our direction for change, for full national consultation. We want all elements in society to help us plan the future. We recognize that this consultative process is itself challenging, too challenging for all too many Members on the other side who cannot resist the temptation to substitute shrill opportunism for real discussion.
Nevertheless, the process is working. More and more groups and individuals are making their views known on the wide range of issues put forward. The Government of the Canadian people is listening because, unlike some Hon. Members opposite, we do not have all the answers! We are listening because we are committed to changing the way the Government goes about making those policies. We were elected to do that and we intend to carry it through.
I noted earlier that there is not much point in trying to prove that a few months' worth of government policies are directly responsible for all the good economic news or for all the bad economic news that could be dredged up to suit a particular debating proposal. That is the kind of game the motion before the House would have us play. However, we take a balanced look at how the economy is progressing and at the various indicators of consumer and business confidence. We find far more reasons for encouragement than for the kind of despair
Supply
that so often emanates from across the floor. And, I might add, we are also a great deal more realistic about how long it will take for the country to overcome all the economic and fiscal problems that were allowed to accumulate.
We have embarked on a long, hard job of rebuilding the foundations for sustained economic growth. To succeed we will have to undo a lot of mistakes that were made in the past by the former Liberal Government. These were mistakes that have become part of the very policy framework that this Government inherited. I do not believe Canadians want another Government that simply moves in and redecorates by papering over the cracks in the walls, and certainly not another Government that uses borrowed money for wallpaper.
We have made a good start on the economic reconstruction that will get the economy growing and producing lasting new jobs for Canadians. The consultation process is in high gear and will remain there until just before the Budget. As well, there is still time for Members opposite to play a more positive role in this process. I hope they will be happy to accept that invitation. At the very least, however, I would ask them to look at all the evidence and come to a balanced view of the current situation on future prospects.
Look at how many new jobs have been created in the past few months and the fact that the unemployment rate is actually below what it was at the beginning of 1984. Look at the third quarter growth rate of 7.6 per cent for the economy. Look at the 1.2 per cent growth rate in real domestic product in November, an annual rate of 15.4 per cent. Look at the increase in manufacturers' shipments and new orders in November, both up by 8 per cent or more on a year-over-year basis. Look at retail sales which are up 10.4 per cent in the same month over a year earlier.
I could go on but my point is not to exhaust the reservoir of encouraging news any more than it is to pretend that every month or every quarter brings nothing but good news. We all know that the economy has serious problems that must be addressed in a serious, long-term way, and that is what the Government has done, is doing and will continue to do throughout its mandate.
While the motion before the House does not deserve to be taken seriously in some basic respects, it does raise some key issues for debate, a debate that we on this side of the House welcome and encourage. At the same time I must regret that the motion displays the same sort of mentality that helped create some of the basic obstacles, and those obstacles are now impeding the renewed growth in the economy and more effective job creation in the country. It is a mentality that attributes to government far more power than it has or should have to do what is best carried out in the private sector by individual Canadians. It is a mentality that, worst of all, would make the past failures of government into an excuse for more of the same old bankrupt Liberal policies of borrow and spend, borrow and spend. That is the policy that has discredited the present situation.
Because of past excesses, a perfectly valid use of government fiscal capacity to support economic growth and job creation

February 12, 1985
Supply
has been severely damaged and will be crippled unless we act to restore fiscal responsibility, confidence and the growth of the private sector where the real jobs for Canadians will be created and sustained. That job is well started but there are no short cuts except those leading to more of the same kind of trouble embodied in the motion before the House.
Since the Hon. Member who moved the motion was not listening at the beginning of my remarks, perhaps I could repeat my quote from Robert Louis Stevenson. It reads as follows:
You cannot run away from a weakness; you must some time fight it out or perish; and if that be so, why not now . .. ?

Mr. Speaker, I have a question to put to the Hon. Minister but first I would like to make a comment. She does not seem to realize that the Opposition motion prepared by a Member of the NDP was directed to the Government. It called on the Government to do certain things and it is not my responsibility or the responsibility of the Liberal Party to respond to an Opposition motion. It is the Government's responsibility. We will participate in this debate but we will participate next. The Minister should be a little more humble while making her first appearance in the House in this debate and making ridiculous statements about who should respond to a motion directed to the Government. She finally did respond to the motion. For a while we did not know whether or not the Government had any response to make.
In her remarks the Minister said, among other things, that unemployment is a serious problem and that it takes two strides to cross a river, that it takes time to solve these problems. She also said that they do not have all of the answers and that they must consult. If that is the case, would she explain why the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), on July 5 in Prince Albert during the election campaign, said: "You are going to see tens upon tens of thousands of jobs being created just as quickly as the new Government can be sworn in"? That is what his Party told the Canadian people during the election campaign. Then it was saying that it had the quick and easy answers. Today the Minister is saying that they must cross the river in two strides; they need time; they must consult. Today she is saying that the Government does not have the answers. It deceived the people during the election campaign. How can the Minister reconcile what she told the House this morning with what her Leader said in Prince Albert on July 5?

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member has not been listening to what we have been saying for the last few months. We have talked directly about jobs. We have talked about jobs throughout the campaign and we have been responsible for at least part of the jobs which have been created since the Government was sworn in. If the Liberal Party were in power, it would take full credit for every single job. We are more modest, Mr. Speaker. We think that there are people in the private sector and in the unions who do have some responsibility and should take some credit for the fact that they are working hard and creating jobs for Canadians.
Jobs have been created this fall. There will be more jobs created this winter, in the spring, on through 1985 and all the way through to 1988. Then in the second term of our mandate there will be more jobs.
I would like to point out that if government spending were the answer to the nation's problems, as the Hon. Member of the Liberal Party would have us understand, then why was unemployment and the deficit proceeding in lock-step toward all-time highs? That point has been made not only by myself but by many private sector economists who really viewed with a jaundiced eye what was happening in the country.
I might also point out that this country is taxed at a higher rate than most other countries and it is very difficult for people in the private sector who are paying these taxes to also create jobs, given the mountain of debt for which they are paying which was created by the former Government. This has been an ongoing problem in this country for 20 years and I think we are turning it around expeditiously.
The Canadian people as well think that we are turning it around expeditiously. The Canadian people have responded very positively. I myself have had 10 or 12 consultations with groups that have expressed faith in the economic agenda and in what we are trying to do. They have all indicated their support not just for what we are trying to do but for the fact that they intend to return to their role in the private sector and provide us with assistance.
I might also point out that in the Province of Newfoundland there have recently been very exciting developments that will lead to more jobs in that province. We all know that the former Government was not able to reach an agreement with that province and that everything was at a standstill. Newfoundland was a province that was discouraged and felt that its resources and challenges were not understood by the federal Government. Now we have a new approach of which we are all very proud. We are proud of the future the agreement will bring and the challenge that has been faced up to by the Government of Newfoundland and the Government of Canada. This was done in order to meet the challenge of the future and to create jobs in a province in which they are desperately needed. There is very little that I can add to what I said in my speech, to the government record in this connection and to the dismal failure by the Liberal Party to provide leadership in this area throughout the years before we took office.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Minister on her efforts, and for pointing out that Saskatchewan should have been mentioned in his motion because of that province's great economic upswing.
There are problems with this motion. The Opposition has spoken about the discredited policies of the Government and that it is opposed to tax increases. I would like to ask the Minister if she supports the payroll tax of the Manitoba Government. That tax is an unnecessary burden on business in Manitoba. Businesses in Manitoba are having a difficult time
February 12, 1985

as it is without having additional taxes imposed on them. I do not understand the motion. The motion states that the New Democratic Party is against taxes, but it does not mention the tax in Manitoba.
When that tax was First introduced, higher interest rates were in effect and consumer purchasing was down. Therefore, businesses could not pass the 1.5 per cent payroll tax on to the consumer. I will speak on this tax in more detail this afternoon. The only thing that tax produced and stimulated was inflation and unemployment. Will the Minister give the assurance to the Elouse that the new Government will not implement a payroll tax similar to the one in Manitoba, which has been detrimental to growth and has caused increased unemployment?

Mr. Speaker, 1 thank the Hon. Member for his question. I would not in any way want to comment on the policies of the Manitoba Government in meeting its agenda. I am sure that Government understands, as does this Government, the difficulties which small and medium-sized businesses are having in meeting payroll taxes. Provincial, federal and municipal Governments all understand that.
Obviously, the Manitoba Government is making its own efforts to meet a difficult situation, as is this Government. The important point which I would like to make in that connection is that we would not dream of suggesting that the Manitoba Government should alter its policies to meet the agenda of this Government. We hope that Hon. Members will understand that the federal Government had a mandate given to it by the Canadian people to meet the challenge of providing jobs for the future. In providing those jobs, this Government expects the same respect from the provinces which it is giving to them. We know it is an important part of the process in Canada, which is a country made up of many strong regions which have different personalities and problems. Every Canadian is very proud of their own particular region or province. We are all trying to meet the same objective-a prosperous Canada which has jobs for all who want and need them.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister has indicated that she is interested in real discussion. Three times during her address she compared the number of jobs which were created since the Conservatives took power to the number of jobs which were created last year. Does the Minister realize that on a month to month basis since the Conservatives took power there have been fewer jobs created in the country than were created during the Turner administration? Does she realize that this Government has created fewer jobs in the country than were created in the last three months of the Trudeau administration? It works out to 33,000 jobs per month under the Turner administration and 32,000 jobs per month in the last three months of the Trudeau administration. However, it works out to 27,000 per month under this administration.
If she is interested in real discussion, she should not compare the figures to those of last year or to those of the Sir John A. Macdonald years. She should be honest about it. Does the Minister realize the flaw in that argument? Will she advise her
Supply
Cabinet colleagues-and in particular the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)-not to use that argument because it is a complete fallacy?

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly aware of the figures which have been cited by the hon. Member. I might point out to him that the Turner administration consisted almost completely of an election campaign. Members on the opposite side of the House were out on the campaign trail, essentially leaving the country to do what it does best, which is to get on with its job in the economy. With the absence of the Liberal Party in Ottawa during the past summer, more jobs were created.

Hear, hear!
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak in this debate on what is considered by Canadians to be the most serious problem in the country today. According to the Gallup poll which was published on January 28, 1985, 56 per cent of those polled said that unemployment was Canada's top problem.
I am not in a position to comment on the Manitoba situation, although I am sure that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) will do that this afternoon. It is my understanding that Manitoba has had success-as opposed to the Conservative provinces-because it took full advantage of several federal programs which were implemented in the last year or two.
While I am not in a position to comment on employment programs in Manitoba, I am in a position to comment on the policies of the present Government. Before and during the election campaign last summer, Conservative Members promised thousands and thousands of jobs. A few minutes ago I cited the statement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made in Prince Albert on July 5. He said that tens upon tens of thousands of jobs would be created as soon as the new Government was sworn in.
If we compare the rhetoric of the election campaign, in relation to jobs, with the speech given today by the Minister- I admit that what the Minister said today was more reasonable-we would conclude that it was deceitful for that Party to make those promises during the election campaign because it gave a pretence to the Canadian people that it had some answers. The Government said that it had the answers, the blueprints and the means by which to solve the problem. Today the Minister quite rightly said that the Government does not have the answers and that it must consult. She said that it takes two strides to cross a river. When I asked her to reconcile her rhetoric today with the rhetoric of the election campaign, she spoke about all sorts of things but never answered the question. The Government does not have the answers. She admitted, as have many Ministers, that it will consult with everybody in the country and that hopefully a consensus will come forward. In other words, the Government will not lead, it will follow the common denominator of the

February 12, 1985
Supply
country and do things on which it will receive a broad consensus, if it can ever do that at all. I say "at all" because we have seen where the consultation process has led so far.
Since the election, what has the Government done about unemployment? The only major thing which it did was reintroduce, immediately after the election, the Canada Works program for this winter. That was a program which was introduced by the Liberal Government. The Government says that it is opposed to direct employment and throwing money at problems, but it did introduce and claim credit for the fact that the Canada Works program was put back in place for the winter. That program is very much similar to the program which we had last winter and the winter before.
What else did the Government do? After two months of procrastination it announced a summer employment program. Most of the elements of that program are very similar to the Summer Canada program of last year, although it has less real dollars and a higher priority for student employment with big business. The Government consulted for two months and ended up with a program which was not very different from the previous program. The program has a different name, and the Government has mixed the elements of that program around a bit, but it put a bigger priority on big business, which is a serious change. It is detrimental to the program. Nevertheless, the Government did not come up with anything startling or new to solve the problem of summer employment. The Government has not put forward a specific or new plan to deal with the unemployment problem.
What has the Government done, Mr. Speaker? It has cut here and cut there. First, it cut the First Chance program which had not simply been promised but had received the approval of the Treasury Board to go ahead. That program would have trained 100,000 young Canadians a year for five years at a cost of $1 billion a year. That program was cut and replaced with a pilot project which would train 4,000 young people a year at a cost of $27 million. So the Government abandoned a program which would have dealt with the problem in a massive way. It still admits the problem is there because it has a pilot project in order to deal with it, but it is a piddling little program called the youth training option which deals with only 4,000 young people at $27 million a year.
Second, the Government cut $432.3 million from the budget of the Department of Employment and Immigration. It cut that money from the Department which is supposed to deal with these problems. Employment assistance and entitlement had $200 million cut; mobility programs had $2.8 million cut; employment services had $1.3 million cut; and general industrial training had $40 million cut. The Summer Canada program was cut and then the Government put it back under a different name with some slight changes. In addition, the Canada student loans program which helps students deal with
training and education was cut by $5 million. The young workers' exchange was cut by $3 million. Environment 2000 which provided jobs in conservation, forest management and environment protection, had $22.8 million cut. The young entrepreneurs' program had $10 million cut. Katimavik, which was an excellent program for young Canadians, had $30 million cut, and Parks Canada had $19.5 million cut.
So in the short period the Conservatives have been in government they have not done one specific new thing at all to solve the unemployment problem. Canada Works, which was our employment program, was put back, but nothing else. Government has cut a lot of programs which were beneficial to the creation of employment. That is its record so far.
PC means "poor Canada".

The Government has no policy, no plan, and it is searching for one now. It does, however, have a general philosophy which has been expressed time and time again by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald).
At this point, I must make one comment. We are having a debate on the problem of unemployment which 56 per cent of Canadians say is the most serious problem in the country, and I must say that 1 am extremely surprised that the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of Finance are not here. We have two Ministers of State present and 1 congratulate them for being here, but it shows the seriousness with which the Government is dealing with this most important problem.

speechtext:
I can't remember that.
February 12, 1985

While the Conservative Government has no programs to deal with unemployment, no specific blueprints and plans, it has enunciated a general policy. That general policy has been that if the Government more or less withdraws from the picture, gets out of direct employment, stops throwing money at the problems, as the Government has put it, then the private sector will come along and create thousands and thousands of jobs. We are told that business will pick up in the areas where the Government pulls back.
Of course, Mrs. Thatcher in England has espoused that philosophy and I believe in England there is an unemployment rate of 13 per cent. I am not saying that that is the only reason for that high unemployment rate, I am sure there are other reasons as well; but to suggest that the answer to the unemployment problem is that sort of philosophical approach is wrong. In the United States it is true that the unemployment rate has come down, but it has come down on the basis of a very strong military and defence construction industry. The manufacturing of armaments in the United States is one area where budgets are being increased, which in turn is propping up employment in that country. But that is a situation where goods are being produced, the purpose of which is to wage war, and I don't believe that in the long run that is the way to solve economic or employment problems.
As a Liberal, I disagree with the basic philosophy being espoused by the Conservative Government. We are told that in time we will see that it will work. 1 doubt that we will ever see it working. I wanted to put this question to the Hon. Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) when she spoke: The Minister of Finance said on November 8 that unemployment will come down only as the United States interest rates fall and, at best, will average 9 per cent for the rest of the decade. What we have here is the Minister of Finance for the Conservative Party telling us that he really cannot do very much about the unemployment problem in Canada, that it will depend on the United States interest rates and, in any case, it is going to stay around 9 per cent for the rest of the decade. Is that the approach of the Conservative Government to unemployment? That is what its Minister of Finance said on November 8.
It's like everything else; it's a made in Washington policy.

Exactly. I would like to point out to this House that the philosophy now being espoused by the Conservative Party is also at variance with the philosophy of the Conservative Party under the leadership of Mr. Clark and Mr. Diefenbaker. Those two Conservative Governments at least believed in direct employment programs. I believe Mr. Diefenbaker in the early 1960s started the winter works program, so he believed in direct employment. But we now have this new conservatism which is withdrawing from that sort of thing in the hope that the private sector will pick up the slack.
I would like to point out that in this country that will not work. The greatest periods of prosperity and job creation we have had in this country have been under what might be called
Supply
mixed economy regimes. That is where Governments have intervened to sustain and promote employment and at the same time help the private sector to expand and to become more productive.
I should point out that during the election campaign the present Prime Minister promised that over the life of his first mandate 552,000 jobs would be created. That would be from the fall of 1984 to approximately the fall of 1988. In the first term of the Trudeau Government, from 1968 to 1972, 800,000 jobs were created. The Minister would say: "Sure, they were created but why should you take credit for that?" I agree with her. But the Conservative Government is now trying to take credit as well for every new job which is created. All we are saying is that if you compare the period from 1968 to 1972, which was Mr. Trudeau's First term in office, you Find that
800,000	jobs were created.
What went wrong after that?

We still maintained a high record. I will give the facts on that and I hope you will still be as enthusiastic as you are now. Canada, even in the 1970s, had the highest record of job creation of all the western countries and there are OPEC Figures to prove that.
Why didn't you continue?

We did continue. The situation was that the very good record of job creation was still not able to deal with the very serious problems in this country which are structural and market-oriented. There are many causes and many complex problems. The Minister today admitted they were complex problems.
It is very interesting to compare some of her statements today with what our Ministers were saying in the House last spring. Those statements are very similar, such as: "It takes time. It's a complex problem. There are many aspects to the unemployment situation in Canada". She is saying that now. However, she and her Party were not saying that during the election campaign.
In any case, to have prosperity in this country, economic growth, high productivity, we need the proper mix of government intervention and private initiative. The Hon. Member across the way from Manitoba can accuse me of being a socialist but I do not pay much attention to that because I know this has been a successful formula over the years. Even if the private sector does pick up and produce a lot of new jobs, and I hope they do, there are a lot of things that have to be done which will never be done by the private sector. There are services for people. The Canada Council on Social Development, appearing before the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration last spring, told us that they had identified in this country over 300,000 jobs which had to be done for Canadians in the area of social services that were not being done. The present chairman of the committee, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), I believe, was on

February 12, 1985
Supply
the committee at that time. These jobs were not being done because the financing was not there to support them, things such as taking care of senior citizens, the illiterate, continuing education, rehabilitation programs for drug and alcohol abusers, slow learner education and programs for native peoples and so on. The private sector is never going to do those kinds of things so they have to be done by governments or agencies supported directly by government.
What can be done? Is it necessary that we in this country live with double-digit unemployment for the rest of this decade or even the 9 per cent that the Minister of Finance seems willing to live with? I do not think so. If we look at some other countries in the world-I know more about them than I do about Manitoba, I hate to admit-the unemployment rate in Austria in 1983 was 4.5 per cent with an inflation rate of 3.8 per cent. It is a relatively small country living next door to an economic giant, West Germany, yet it is able to maintain through a mixed economy system a relatively low rate of unemployment and inflation.
In Japan, a completely different type of country, the unemployment rate in 1983 was 2.7 per cent and inflation was 1.8 per cent. That is a very interesting situation because Japan is very much into new technology, robots and automation. Some Canadians argue that if we bring in new technology we are going to have a higher rate of unemployment. Well, here you have Japan, a leader in the world, with 2.7 per cent unemployment. In 1983 Norway had 3.3 per cent unemployment and Sweden 3.5 per cent. So it can be done.
In the short time I have left, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that I personally believe, as I have recommended in several other Budget debates in the last couple of years, that we should have a six and five program for unemployment. Make the same effort in unemployment that we made in inflation when we brought it down from 12 per cent or 13 per cent to what it is now, 4 per cent or 5 per cent. We made it the highest priority and put a lot of effort into it. I think we should do the same for unemployment and we can do it through a mixed program.
To begin with, Mr. Speaker, we help the private sector become as efficient and productive as possible, even if that means the loss of jobs in certain manufacturing sectors. By doing that we will keep those wealth producers in Canada. We will not lose them by maintaining an inefficient system. We help them adapt to the new technology so they can compete with these other countries. Then we put a lot more money into retraining and upgrading so that people displaced by this new approach and the changes in our industry and economy will be redirected into those new jobs and trained accordingly. That requires not pilot projects of $27 million, it requires programs of $1 billion a year. It requires a lot of money but it is an investment in the economy of the country.
In addition to that we also need changes in our work time schedules. Through a greater emphasis on education by way of student loans and government support for education, there would be a delayed entry of young people into the workforce if they were all getting the education they really require. We
should also, through encouragement and incentive, allow people who want to retire early to do so so they can leave the workforce and young people can come in at the bottom and get some of those jobs. We know that under the new Charter of Rights it will be illegal or unconstitutional forcibly to put a man out of work just because he is 65 or 60, or whatever it is; but we can have incentive programs for early retirement. I know they are being studied now and they are very important to this whole subject.
We could also encourage part-time work which has all the benefits of full-time work so people who want to train for part of the week or take care of families can also work. If we properly supported part-time work it would also leave open some jobs for other people to work at. In addition, we should support the recommendations of the many reports relating to paid educational leave for skills upgrading and training.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe the problem can be solved. We can bring down unemployment because it has been done in the countries I referred to. But it will not be done if the Government continues to follow the philosophy it has been espousing so far. I say philosophy because I cannot criticize the Government for the programs it has put forward; there have been very few programs. However, I urge the Government to look at what is being done in other parts of the world and to listen to some of the comments being made.
There was a very interesting program last night on The Journal where a number of economists from Canada and the U.S. were discussing these very matters. Many of them were putting forward recommendations similar to what I am putting forward today. In any case, except for the man from McLeod, Young, Weir Limited, they did not agree with the philosophy that seems to be espoused by the Government. Therefore I urge the Government through this motion to take seriously the demands being made, that in its consultations it does not put on blinkers but looks at some of the things being done in places which have been successful in bringing down the unemployment rate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions and comments?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is a very active Member and chairman of the Special Committee on Employment which went across this country a few years ago and produced an excellent report. I want his opinion on the program announced last week, the special Student Employment and Experience Development program. Does he think it is really going to be adequate, especially in rural areas of this country?
Under that program the Government allocated $165 million to offices only. If you are in a rural area like Algoma or Manitoulin, then the funds will be allocated perhaps to Sudbury or Sault Ste. Marie. The rural communities and businesses, Indian bands, municipalities and non-profit groups will really be in competition with much larger groups from half a dozen districts. In the past ridings like Algoma would have an allocation of, say, $968,000 and now they really have none. A similar allocation would provide about 100 projects and 500
February 12, 1985

jobs. Now there is really no allocation so there is really no guarantee that those rural municipalities and other groups will receive any amount of funding. I really wonder whether this is advantageous to rural municipalities.
The other problem that I see in rural areas, and I am sure the Hon. Member would have some advice on this, is that in slow growth areas of the country where the economy is not very strong I wonder whether the private sector will use that program because they have to put up half the funding. Instead of providing additional assistance for hard-pressed areas, those funds will flow into areas which are relatively better off and have more prosperous businesses that can take advantage of the program.
By the same token, in the past municipalities received 100 per cent of the funding. They now have to provide 25 per cent of the compulsory contributions and all of the equipment costs. In the past that was all provided: a small municipality could employ three or four people and get $7,000 to $10,000 in funding. They now receive only 75 per cent of the funding to assist in training students. I believe we will be short of funds in rural areas.
Under the old Summer Canada program there were a lot of funds available through the departmental stream for Indian bands. In my constituency there are about 12 bands with 7,000 or 8,000 status Indians. They will now have to compete with businessmen from big cities such as North Bay and Sudbury. In the past they were able to apply for funding through the Department of Indian Affairs. The Hon. Member has had a lot of experience in this. Does he really believe that this program will be fair in assisting the slow growth areas where unemployment has hit the hardest, such as in northern Ontario, certain areas of the Maritimes and northern Quebec? Is this funding going to be gobbled up by the rich municipalities and businesses in the faster moving and more economically sound areas of the country?

Mr. Speaker, in the last Parliament there was the Task Force on Employment Opportunities for the '80s made up of seven Members of Parliament; four from the Government, two from the Conservative Party, and one from the NDP. We travelled extensively throughout the country and met with business organizations, unions, universities and community groups. We worked for over a year and then produced a report. It was made very clear in the report that direct employment programs were necessary. It was also made clear in our recommendations that there had to be a mix between government support for private sector employment and for community and municipal employment creation.
The Member makes a good point. In the announcement made the other day of $205 million for the summer employment program, there was no specific allocation of money for community organizations and municipalities as opposed to the private sector. As a matter of fact, the Minister said that there was a priority for summer employment with the private sector and, in particular, with big business in the private sector.

There are many parts of Canada where the big business private sector is not strong. In some areas such as the Gaspe, parts of Atlantic Canada, northern Ontario and Quebec it is non-existent. Yesterday in the House I asked the Minister to reconsider and put aside a good percentage of that money for community groups and municipalities.
Let us look at the allocation made under that student summer employment program. Out of the $200 million provided last year, Newfoundland got $5.5 million; this year it will only get $5.1 million. Last year Nova Scotia got $6.2 million; this year it will only get $5.7 million. Prince Edward Island received $1.2 million last year; this year it will get $.7 million. Last year New Brunswick got $5.8 million; this year it will only get $4.9 million. Last year Quebec got $43.7 million; this year it will only get $41.9 million. Every province east of Ontario will receive less money this year. Due to equalization the poorer provinces of Canada, which need help the most, are getting less money. I do not know how that is justified.
Another interesting point is that right after the Minister announced her program, executives of several of the big companies which she had consulted with said that they could not make any commitment to hire the thousands of young people that they were expected to. They said that they would try. A Noranda official said: "You can't hire students when you are laying off their mothers and fathers. At worst, Noranda expects to hire 100 students more than the 1,300 they hired last year, but the number depends on business increases". Students will be ready for work around April 15. They are relying on jobs with the big corporations. I do not know what students will do in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and northern Ontario.
