speakeroldname: Mr. Dan McKenzie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak on this NDP motion. They are criticizing policies of tax increases and spending cuts, but they fail to make any criticism of the NDP Government which implemented a regressive anti-labour tax in Manitoba. It is called the Manitoba payroll tax. It has even been severely criticized by some of the most left-wing journalists in Manitoba. In order to cope with this tax, businesses in Manitoba have had to lay off people to cover the cost of the payroll tax which they have to pay to the NDP Government. I visited businesses in Manitoba which are expanding. It was explained to me that they could hire more people in their plants if it were not for this regressive Manitoba payroll tax. This has discouraged businesses from investing in Manitoba. They preferred to go to provinces which did not have this payroll tax. Farmers have to pay this tax as well, as though they did not have enough problems to contend with.
I see the coalition is working today. There they are, huddling again, just like they did between 1972 and 1974. I am

February 12, 1985
Supply
sure the Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) will remember what happened in those days.

We are looking at the new Whip
appointments.
You didn't make it, Dan. You're not going to be a Whip.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The NDP supported the Liberals 19 times in a row to bring about economic chaos in this country during that period. The NDP Government in Manitoba is removing the hydro rates freeze which was put in place by the previous Conservative Government. As a result hydro rates have increased. This increase in hydro rates was another shock for businesses and farmers since during the election campaign Premier Pawley promised that the freeze would not be lifted.
So much for NDP campaign promises. This regressive antilabour tax forced Kimberley-Clark to leave the Province of Manitoba. It is now expanding in Ontario where there is no 1.5 per cent payroll tax. Shell Oil closed its plant in Manitoba because it is just too expensive to stay in business under the NDP Government in Manitoba.
Cut-backs are mentioned in this motion. However, nothing is said about the Finance Minister of Manitoba announcing that he would make cut-backs. If cut-backs have such a negative effect on employment, why is the NDP not criticizing their colleagues in Manitoba? This motion should condemn them for the cuts if they will cause unemployment.
In an announcement in November, the senior Cabinet Minister confirmed that the provincial Treasury Board had asked Cabinet Ministers to scrutinize certain expenditures and submit programs and services that could be cut back or limited. There is not much consistency in the motion. The NDP condemns taxes but condones provincial NDP increases in taxes in Manitoba. There is no comment about the Minister of Finance there who is introducing cut-backs.
I received a document today from the Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses. They realize that the uncontrolled spending must be brought under control. They state in their brief:
Although CFIB suggestions for modifying the tax system are not costly in national terms, we suggest the following area where the small business community can and should contribute to the government's efforts to reduce the size of the federal deficit.
I commend that association for realizing that something must be done.
I am not in favour of commonly using the word "cut-back" because it is actually the elimination of waste, mismanagement and duplication. That is what we on this side are trying to do and it is something that was never done under successive Liberal Governments. One only needs to read the Auditor General's Report, which gets worse every year, to have evidence of uncontrolled spending. Now that the Liberals are in opposition they have an immediate answer for everything.
One of the most amusing scenes I have ever seen was during the Liberal leadership campaign last summer. During that leadership campaign one would think that the Liberals had been in opposition for 20 years because each candidate had a solution for everything. If that was the case I do not understand why we have unemployment and huge deficits today. The Liberals have been in power for 20 years with majorities during some of that time. If they had all the answers, why did they not implement all those policies in order to prevent unemployment and the high deficit?
Let us review how unemployment originally began. Between 1972 and 1975 when the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) was the Minister of Finance, the number of unemployed rose by 164,000 and youth unemployment climbed by 109,000. This became worse over the years until the number of unemployed at this time is 1.5 million. Where were all the brilliant policies and why were they not implemented at that time? Obviously the Liberals had the wrong policies.
In that twenty-ninth Parliament the NDP supported the Liberals in 19 consecutive non-confidence motions. During the election campaign I heard a very interesting comment on Radio Station CJOB in Winnipeg. A very prominent New Democrat said on the radio that the best governments are minority governments. Unemployment increased by 164,000 and youth unemployment climbed by 109,000 during a minority government. Is that what the NDP describe as good government?
While there are no quick fixes or instant solutions, we are certainly making great strides. The energy agreement in Newfoundland yesterday was certainly well received by the people of that province and it will create much employment. Furthermore, the economic conference and the First Ministers' conference will produce more plans with regard to creating employment. When the energy agreement is reached with the western provinces, more employment will be created at that time. We will not implement another disastrous energy policy which caused so many problems for all of Canada, particularly the west.
While we are being told about the prosperity in Manitoba, we are not hearing the same comments from the business community. Let me quote John Bulloch, President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, in an article in the Winnipeg Free Press:
Manitoba's New Democratic Party government is the most anti-business regime in Canada, John Bulloch, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, said yesterday.
"It still hasn't dawned on this government that the new jobs and Manitoba's hopes for a better future depend largely on a revitalized small and medium-sized business sector," he told a news conference one day after the federation's annual meeting, held in Winnipeg this year.
"The government of Manitoba clings to the lame philosophy that only it can solve all the problems and that only it can breathe new life into its sick economy."
"Manitoba seems blind to the fact that its policies are doing just the opposite."
February 12, 1985

He said 60 per cent of the federation's members in Manitoba implemented pay cuts or pay freezes while the province increased the salaries of public servants by about 10 per cent.
Therefore, not everyone agrees that it is all milk and honey in Manitoba. I recall that in 1969 we had a balanced budget in Manitoba. There was stability in the country and there was steady growth. Subsequently, all Hades broke loose in that province in regard to the budget deficit that has been increasing and causing very serious problems there.
Furthermore, the NDP like to give the impression that they are the only ones interested in health care. That is not true. That Government's regressive payroll tax in Manitoba has even affected rural hospitals. An article in the Winnipeg Sun on December 10, 1982 states:
Municipal taxpayers may have to bail out rural hospitals that are being swamped with red ink because of the province's payroll tax.
Several hospital administrators said yesterday that the payroll tax is swelling their deficits and they don't know where they are going to get the money.
It is as if our hospitals don't have enough problems!
"The 1.5 per cent payroll tax is killing us," said one administrator who did not want to be identified. "Taxpayers aren't going to be happy about seeing a hospital tax."
Carman Memorial Hospital is typical of what is happening in many facilities across the province. The hospital pays $1,000 each month in payroll taxes and that only adds to the burden of a deficit hovering in the range of $50,000.
This additional $1,000 a month is being imposed on hospitals in small towns across the province. If that is not regressive and anti-labour, I don't know what is.
One of the strongest supporters of the New Democratic Party in Manitoba is Frances Russell, a columnist for the Winnipeg Free Press. She is a very strong left-wing socialist and certainly does not try to hide that fact. She recently stated in her column that "Pawley's payroll tax is no laughing matter. A regressive, anti-labour tax like this certainly is no laughing matter.
She states:
-the payroll tax is emerging as the new government's biggest embarrassment. It may even turn into a political disaster.
Let me tell the House that the Leader of the Opposition in Manitoba, the Hon. Gary Filmon, has stated that when he forms the next government, one of his first measures will be to remove this regressive anti-labour tax. We certainly hope that the NDP will summon enough courage to call an election in the near future so that we can remove this tax.
Frances Russell also states:
More importantly, the tax is proving to be a particularly bad move now that unemployment has become the number one political and economic issue in Canada. Manitoba's unemployment rate has risen 75 per cent in the past year-
About the second lowest increase in Canada.
During the last election campaign, as in previous electoral battles, the NDP has presented itself as the party that cares about the individual entrepreneur. Yet this tax bears most heavily on precisely that community, particularly in a recession when many small businesses are fighting to stave off bankruptcy.
That was a very regressive tax. The huge deficit in Manitoba was brought about entirely by the NDP because we had a
Supply
balanced budget in 1969. This is hurting Manitoba's financial rating. Manitoba's financial position has deteriorated significantly over the last two years. A major New York ratings house stated yesterday that it had lowered the province's credit rating. Standard and Poor's dropped Manitoba's rating from AA to AA-minus. They also dropped the rating for Manitoba Hydro.
Talk about fancy bookkeeping, Mr. Speaker! We talk about the Auditor General's report here; it is not any better in Manitoba. Mr. Ziprick, Manitoba's Auditor General, has stated that the deficit in Manitoba is unreal. In an article in the Winnipeg Free Press we read:
The auditor also took issue with another of the government's accounting practices relating to the Crown-owned Manitoba Forestry Resources Ltd. in The Pas.
Ziprick said the province wrote off a $51.3 million liability Manfor owed to the government in November, 1983. The investment was initially made in 1973 after the province had taken over the old Churchill Forest Industries.
The $51.3 million should have been considered a government expenditure at the time instead of being carried on the books at all these years, Ziprick said-
The government's public accounts also show Manitoba spent almost $270 million last year on financial charges stemming from the province's total debt-
The province's net combined debt is almost $6 billion or about $6,000 for each man, woman and child.
We have nothing to learn from the NDP Government in Manitoba.
In closing, I want to point out to the people of Manitoba, who will want to remember this at the next provincial election, that the provincial debt is rising under the NDP in Manitoba by $81 every minute. That is a sad, sick record of a very sick, socialist government and we certainly will not be implementing anything it would recommend in our Budget.
Some Liberals mentioned that there was no funding going to municipalities in the cities, that they are all cut off.
That is right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The Lyon Government was unable in four years to correct the huge deficit which was run up by the Schreyer Government and the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) should know that. He has been around here long enough. I would like to read all the debt figures into the record today but we are limited to 20 minutes. I could have explained it to him in a lot more detail. We will have such a debt in this country unless we take some very positive steps because it will just get out of control. The New Democratic Party is about the only group that feels that we should do nothing about this huge deficit, but there is no way that the Lyon Government could correct eight years of Schreyer in four years.

Mr. Speaker, does not the Hon. Member realize that every Government in Canada, the federal Government and all the provincial Governments, are all operating with deficits; that the deficit is caused mainly by the fact that we have so much unemployment, that more than 11 per cent of the working population is not working, which means they are
not earning money? They are not drawing wages or salary and, therefore, they are not paying income tax. As a result people are not purchasing goods and services which other people produce. Rather than adding to the economy, they are costing the economy through payments of welfare and unemployment insurance.
Does the Member not realize that if governments of whatever stripe were to attack the deficit by really cutting back expenditures at a time when the private sector is not providing the jobs that are required, we would have even more unemployment, tens of thousands, indeed hundreds of thousands of people either drawing unemployment insurance or welfare, and in this kind of economy no government whatever its political stripe can really do much about reducing the deficit?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have proven beyond the shadow of a doubt in this country that this philosophy of the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party that you solve all problems either by spending more money, borrowing more money, or going into debt has not worked. If that were the answer, we would not have 1.3 million people unemployed. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North is overlooking completely that the money has not been spent wisely. Billions and billions of dollars have been absolutely wasted. Billions of dollars have been thrown at different programs. These programs were not well thought out. There was no consultation.
This is one of the problems we have had in Canada under the Liberals. They governed by confrontation. They spent money without consultation with the private sector and the provinces. That is why we are being so well received by the business community and the provinces. They are saying that it is a refreshing change to be able to sit down and discuss these programs in advance instead of having the federal Government forcing issues. We have to exercise caution in regard to the size of the debt and the borrowing. The policies of the Liberal Government over the years have just driven billions of dollars of investment money out of the country.
This sort of thing has done the economy in places like Kentucky a lot of good. Kentucky advertises itself as the eleventh province because so much Canadian money has gone there. The same thing has happened in Florida, California and the Carolinas. More has been done for the economy in the States than in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Government is perpetrating yet another vicious attack upon public servants in the National Capital Region. Not content with cutting thousands of jobs, sending everyone into a state of panic, and increasing unemployment, especially among women, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) is performing another raid upon the pocketbook of public servants by increasing parking fees for government employees from $42 to $75 and, in some cases, to $85 per month. This increase of 100 per cent and more is perpetrated in many cases upon people of modest means, sole support parents, and many others who cannot afford it.
The Government preaches restraint. Does the Minister of Public Works worry about public servants? No. Do Tory Members from Ottawa-Carleton, Ottawa West, Nepean-Carleton, Gatineau, and others worry? No, they do not. They have not said a word on this issue.
The Government is overcharging public servants and uses the money to pay for its extravagance and comfort, with 40 limousines, 40 chauffeurs, 40 political commissars, and a fleet of jets flying around delivering copies of speeches of Cabinet Ministers. This is Robin Flood in reverse. The Government is taking from the poor and giving to the rich-itself.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am most distressed at a comment appearing in the Saturday, February 9, edition of The Toronto Star and attributed to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). It is beyond the realm of possibility that the Right Hon. Member could have made such a racist statement. I know he is aware of the broad spectrum make-up of the Conservative Party. He is also familiar with the diverse ethnic and religious constituency represented by the Conservative Governments both in Ottawa and in the provinces. Persons of all races, creeds, and colours are welcome in the Conservative Party, as the Leader of the Opposition well knows.
I call for the Right Hon. Member to rise in his place at three o'clock today to confirm, correct, or deny this shameful statement.

Mr. Speaker, in 1977 the subcommittee on the penitentiary system in Canada made a very clear-cut recommendation which read as follows:
Retirement at 55 years of age must be mandatory for all employees other than professional staff, with full pension after 25 years of service. Early voluntary retirement at age 50 after 20 years of service should be optional.
I am now calling upon the Government to recognize the exceptional pressures and stresses which are part of every day life for a penitentiary guard in a maximum security institution. The present pension structure for RCMP officers and Armed Forces personnel recognizes the extra stress of those jobs. The pension plan of air traffic controllers also recognizes a tension syndrome peculiar to that group.
The statistics on shorter life expectancy for the custodial service point to the need for immediate remedial measures. I call upon the Government to take the initiative where the Liberals failed, and to carry out the recommendation made years ago and agreed to by all three political Parties as late as last June. I call upon the Government to introduce immediately legislation to allow this group early retirement.

maintopic: PRICE OF GASOLINE-SUGGESTED FULLSCALE REVISION OF TAX SYSTEMS
PRICE OF GASOLINE-SUGGESTED FULLSCALE REVISION OF TAX SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on the premiums and bonuses being offered to consumers by the oil companies. I think they should lower the price of gas instead of giving away hamburgers, glasses, dishes and discounts on cigarettes. Consumers in Beauce and Quebec are fed up with constant increases in the price of gas. They want to pay less per litre, they don't want premiums.
Why should the Quebec consumer let himself be skinned by the multinationals and the tax system without demanding an explanation, especially since last week, Canadian oil companies announced record profits? Quebecers feel they are getting a raw deal and they want to know what is going on.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest an overall review of our tax systems.
In the United States, where taxation is not as severe and oil producers engage in healthy competition instead of conspiring to "skin" the consumer, the price of gas is dropping everywhere. At this very moment, even considering the value of the U.S. dollar and the fact that their gallon is not as big as ours, it still works out to about $1.65 per gallon. In other words, almost $1 less than over here.
Canadians may rest assured that Progressive Conservative Members will work hard to protect consumers, whether they live in Beauce, in Quebec or elsewhere in Canada. It is up to us

February 12, 1985
to act, and I am confident that our Government will find a fair and equitable solution.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of the fishermen of the great northern peninsula of Newfoundland and Labrador, and on behalf of the many development associations, fishermen's committees, and community councils, which spent a great deal of time, effort, and money to organize, on a very large scale, a conference to be held in the northern peninsula community of St. Anthony at the end of this month, to discuss the future of the Fisheries of that area.
The meeting had been arranged. People had committed themselves to travel hundreds of miles to be at the meeting. An agenda had been set. Everything was in place. The fisheries of the northern peninsula of Newfoundland and Labrador are the most underdeveloped anywhere in the country. With the formation of a new federal-provincial fish company, it is now critical that special attention be paid to this area. The people on this coast, in the highest unemployment area anywhere in the nation, deserve the time and attention of the federal Minister of Fisheries. Furthermore, they deserve respect, especially for their efforts to organize the meeting. I plead with the Minister, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and Newfoundland's regional Minister to assure their attendance at the earliest possible-
I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member.

subtopic: CHALLENGE '85-ENTHUSIASM IN TEMISCAMINGUE OVER PROGRAM ANNOUNCEMENT
CHALLENGE '85-ENTHUSIASM IN TEMISCAMINGUE OVER PROGRAM ANNOUNCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week on February 6, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) presented her student summer employment program called Challenge 85. This program, with a total budget of $205 million, is to create 95,000 jobs for next summer.
Mr. Speaker, this announcement certainly cooled off Members of the two Opposition parties who have been harrassing and criticizing our Minister for more than two months, despite patient insistence by the Minister of Employment and Immigration and our Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) that in due time, they would be bringing in a program that was better structured, better designed and especially better adapted to the needs of students and young people.
Mr. Speaker, this program is unique in that it appeals more particularly to the private sector and our municipalities to show their confidence in students by giving them a chance to acquire practical training.
Mr. Speaker, on the weekend I held a number of consultations in my riding. I met with businessmen, representatives of chambers of commerce and municipal authorities, all of whom were quite enthusiastic, and I can assure you that in Temiscamingue, we are ready to meet "Challenge 85".

Mr. Speaker, we in the New Democratic Party, as do all reasonable Canadians, rejoice that finally there is an agreement between Canada and Newfoundland to pave the way for the development of the Hibernia oil field.
Yesterday I was in Corner Brook, watching the signing ceremony on television. A Newfoundlander next to me said: "Those boys are going to get sore arms from patting themselves on the back so much". Be that as it may, I am glad there has been an agreement.
I have three positive suggestions. First, we should consider a constitutional amendment to enshrine provincial control of offshore resources in the Constitution. As a western Canadian, I realize how important that is. Second, we have to be careful about the pace of development and about the creation of jobs. Energy, Mines and Resources officials told the energy committee this year that there would only be 6,000 jobs in the development of the field. Expectations are very high. Let us have some hearings by the energy committee to see if we can get more jobs, and to see whether we can get some jobs for western Newfoundland and Labrador which often feel left out of the development.
Finally, I would urge that the federal and provincial Governments not forget the traditional industries like fisheries and forestry where there really are jobs for the future. I am glad that there is a deal. Let us work on it and try to create more and better jobs. Let us not forget the fish and the forests as well.
February 12, 1985

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals in this House, who are Members of a Party that wasted public funds for fifteen years and who represent what remains of the previous Government's institutional arrogance, make it impossible for us to forget their legacy. Our forest industry, for instance, is in great difficulty, and I am therefore very pleased with the particular emphasis placed on this sector by the present government. In a matter of weeks, I think we can guarantee the people of Quebec, of whom 250,000 work in this sector, that the sectoral agreement will meet the forest industry's essential requirements relating to research, management and all forestry problems.
Mr. Speaker, it is therefore important to emphasize consultation, as our Government is doing now, and help 250,000 forestry workers in Quebec, who, just as our senior citizens and students, may be assured our Government will "deliver the goods".

subtopic: CANADIAN FEDERATION OF AGRICULTURE-FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY MEETING
CANADIAN FEDERATION OF AGRICULTURE-FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I would like to call attention to the 50th anniversary meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture which is taking place in Hull, here in the National Capital area. We welcome the delegates to the capital of our country and to Parliament this week.
The CFA represents the producers of many agricultural commodities and tens of thousands of farmers across the country. The contributions which the CFA has made over the last half century to Canadian agriculture have been very great. We pay tribute to its many members who have given so generously of their time.
The CFA has called on the Government to reinstate the Canadian Agriculture Export Corporation which has been so successful in its first few months of operation, selling $16 million worth of commodities and making arrangements for additional sales of $100 million. However, the Government has sold out to the multinational agriculture exporting corporations so it is destroying Canagrex, a company we designed to help farmers sell their commodities abroad.
Canagrex is especially important at a time when countries like the United States and others are more aggressively marketing their commodities abroad. I call on the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Government to start listening to the farmers and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture,
and to stop listening to the powerful multinational agriculture trading companies which are only interested in their own profits, not in the farmers of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in Stormont-Dundas time is a very important commodity. When we have a meeting at three o'clock, we have a meeting at three o'clock. If the meeting starts before three, then the meeting starts early. If the meeting starts after three, then the meeting starts late. There is no confusion. Even my five-year old son Michael recognizes that when the little hand is at three and the big hand is at twelve, the time is three o'clock.
In Ottawa there appears to be some confusion about time, or possibly some lack of respect for time. Many meetings do not start when scheduled because participants habitually arrive late. If a meeting is called for three o'clock, the general attitude appears to be that the commencement time is not really three o'clock but perhaps 3.05, 3.10 or 3.20.
I can offer two solutions. We could consider that Ottawa be in a different time zone and agree that everyone would be 10 or 20 minutes late. There are some obvious problems with this concept. Perhaps we should consider the simplest solution. Everyone should agree that three o'clock means three o'clock, four o'clock means four o'clock, and so on. If we agree to meet at a certain time, then we have made a definite commitment and we should feel obligated to meet at that specific time.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO PERSONS AGED 16 AND 17 YEARS
APPLICATION TO PERSONS AGED 16 AND 17 YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the great achievements of the last Parliament was the Young Offenders Act. On April 1, the Young Offenders Act is supposed to come into effect to include all 16 and 17-year olds across the country.
I learned this morning that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) intends, when he is in Regina, to announce that that law will not apply to 16 and 17-year olds. I know that he has had considerable pressure from some provincial Governments not to let the law apply to these young people but to continue dealing with those young people under the adult system. I would remind the Prime Minister that the setting of that age is a federal matter and that the Parliament of Canada acted unanimously. Members of the Conservative, NDP, and Liberal Parties all agreed that 16 and 17-year olds should fall under the juvenile justice system and that that system should be toughened up, and it was toughened up.
I would call on the Prime Minister not to take this step backward, and remind him that there is legal opinion to the

February 12, 1985

effect that it would be unlawful to exclude 16 and 17-year olds from the Act in some parts of the country though they are included in others once the equality provisions of the Charter of Rights come into effect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some extremely serious questions to ask of the Prime Minister. The Government is finding itself in a very messy situation at this time when one of the major newspapers of Canada is saying that the Solicitor General of Canada has acted with bad judgment in the execution of his functions, and now we read in a paper that the Minister of National Defence has put himself in a very embarrassing situation that could involve our national security. In light of this, when will the Prime Minister take these
problems seriously, stop being a nice guy, and make the tough decisions that the Prime Minister is supposed to make?

subsubtopic: NEWSPAPER REFERENCE TO MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as my hon. friend very inelegantly and inaccurately makes a reference to a statement in the papers, I should respond in regard to one serious matter that was mentioned and that, of course, is the question of national security, to use the term used by my hon. friend. When the allegations were first brought to my attention, I immediately, within moments, initiated a series of inquiries and assured myself that at no time and under no circumstances was the national security of Canada compromised in any way. Having said that, I want to tell the House that my hon. friend, the Minister of National Defence, will be making a statement in the House at three o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the statement by the Minister, and I am happy that he will be in the House to make a statement, I think it would be in the public interest to know when the Prime Minister was informed of the incident and who informed him. Was it the Clerk of the Privy Council, the Chief of Staff, or was it any person from the NATO organization?

Mr. Speaker, I was informed by an appropriate official of the Government of Canada. I responded within minutes of that information being made available to me. I secured the assurances which I have just imparted to the House. I know that my hon. friend, in the interests of fairness, will want to wait for the statement of the Hon. Minister of National Defence.

Mr. Speaker, with respect, I would like to point out to the Right Hon. Prime Minister that the questions we are asking at this time are not directed to the Minister of National Defence. We want to know what the reaction was of the Prime Minister of Canada and the attitude he took, because this is a very important matter involving Canada's reputation with its NATO allies. I would therefore like to know whether it is correct that the Right Hon. Prime Minister was informed of these events in November or early December and why he has not acted until today.

Mr. Speaker, in spite of the assurance I gave the House, the Hon. Member insists on insinuating that a matter of national security was not dealt with. I have already given the House the assurance that moments after the information or the allegations were brought to my attention, I acted immediately in order to be in a position to give the House and my colleagues
February 12, 1985

the assurance that there was no national security problem of any kind whatsoever.
That being said, I know Hon. Members will want to hear the Minister's statement at three o'clock this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, we are talking about the national security of Canada. It is a very serious question. What did Canada's Chief of Defence Staff report to the Prime Minister about the allegations which are outlined in today's Ottawa Citizen, and when did he tell the Prime Minister? What did the Clerk of the Privy Council report to the Prime Minister about the allegations which are outlined in today's press, and when did he tell the Prime Minister? Finally, did Lord Carrington, Secretary General of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, during his visit to Canada in late January, or any other NATO official, tell the Prime Minister or any other Canadian official about these very serious national security allegations?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague asked if Lord Carrington or any other NATO official brought this to my attention. The answer is in the negative in both cases. As I indicated to my hon. friend, the information was brought to my attention by an appropriate official of the Government of Canada, and I immediately acted upon it in regard to the question of national security.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. It is obvious that the Prime Minister has known about these allegations for some time. It is also obvious, from what he has said, that he has been informed about them. Why has it taken the Prime Minister weeks, or maybe two months, to react? Why did he not act prior to this particular moment when he is pressured into it by the media? Does the Prime Minister not realize that national security matters can affect our country's national security with our NATO partners, that he must act now, and that he should have acted previously?

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend does the House a disservice. In response to a direct and important question, I indicated to my hon. friend that, immediately upon receipt of the information, I acted to assure myself and the Government that there had been no breach of security of any kind. That having been done, I think my hon. friend would also agree that it is important that individuals in this House, or elsewhere, not be tried- except in serious matters of national security-in regard to innuendo and unsubstantiated allegations. I can assure Members of the House that I acted with propriety and celerity to ensure that all information related to the suggestion of national security was dealt with properly.

subsubtopic: RESIGNATION OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a statement before my peers and my Prime Minister. This afternoon I have tendered my resignation as Minister of National Defence to the Prime Minister.
An article published today in an Ottawa newspaper contains many inaccuracies and those inaccuracies are wrong, libellous and even suggest a breach of security. I have retained counsel and can give you the assurance, Mr. Speaker, that an action has been started against the paper in question.
I have assured the Prime Minister of my innocence and my conduct. I have served in the House for 28 years. I have served under three Prime Ministers. I have always respected the House, its membership and its traditions.
I also recognize the fundamental importance of my portfolio, one which is as sensitive as any in government. I am a man of honour who respects Parliament and I especially respect my Prime Minister. Accordingly, I have resigned as Minister of National Defence, effective today.

That this House commends the Government of Manitoba for its positive policies of job creation which have produced the lowest unemployment level in Canada, and calls upon the Government to adopt a similar course of economic expansion rather than the discredited policies of tax increases and spending cuts which it has pursued to date and which are largely responsible for the latest unemployment statistics, which show an alarming increase of 167,000 unemployed between December, 1984 and January, 1985.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to comment in reply to the speech made by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) prior to lunch. He stated in the House that his Government had a very good employment policy. The Conservatives may feel that they have a good employment policy. I would like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it depends on whose employment you are talking about. I am reading the list of political appointments that have been made since the election on September 4. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Government House Leader)
speechtext: Without pay.

There definitely is a government make-work policy here. It works well for all Conservative Members. I am glad to hear the Parliamentary Secretary saying "without pay". I would like to know whether the former Tory Member of Parliament who was appointed the Ambassador for Disarmament was appointed without pay; whether Mr. Robert Byron who was given interim supervision of the advertising management group was also hired without pay; whether Mr. Paul Marshall and Mr. Lucien Bouchard were appointed without pay; whether Mr. Lawrence Hanigan was hired without pay.
There seems to be a very good employment strategy but I would like to argue that it is relatively selective. In other words, it seems that you have to be either a defeated Tory candidate or a former member of the Tory caucus in order to avail yourself of these employment opportunities. All this comes from a Government which has stated time and time again that it did not want to partake in partisan things, and that it wanted to have a parliamentary committee review political appointments.
Those are the comments I wanted to make in reply to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine. I disagree with what he said and I disagree totally with the remarks regarding the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner). speechtext: We will now resume debate. The period for questions and comments has terminated.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate today on an Opposition motion concerning the disastrous unemployment situation in Canada. Considering the concern all Canadians have for this very serious problem, it is entirely appropriate that the Opposition, and I want to thank the Hon. Member who moved this motion, should draw the attention of the Government to the gravity of the unemployment situation in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I see to my dismay there are no Ministers in the House. I think there is a rule that there must be at least one Minister to take part in the debate. Mr. Speaker, if I were so inclined, I would even raise the question of whether we have a quorum, but I will refrain for the time being.
Mr. Speaker, before the election on September 4, the Progressive Conservative Party's slogan was: "Jobs, jobs,

February 12, 1985
Supply
jobs". They bored us all summer with that kind of stuff, claiming that as soon as they were elected, tens of thousands of jobs would be created in Canada and that the unemployed would at last find lucrative and productive employment. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, since this Government was elected, the results have been sad in the extreme. During the initial months of their mandate, they took credit for the results of policies introduced by the previous Administration. The gradual drop in unemployment we experienced at the same time was certainly due to those policies, and they used those results to very good advantage. Now, however, after several months of Conservative Government, we can see what the unemployment trend is going to be. Between December 1984 and January 1985, 167,000 men, women and young people lost their jobs, and the unemployment rate rose from 10.9 to 11.2 per cent. Since then, we have not heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) quoting statistics or the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) talking about job creation. We have not seen any backbenchers bragging as they were doing last fall when they took the credit for figures that were encouraging. Now that the situation is deteriorating they seem to have been struck dumb.
Last month, another 53,000 young Canadians lost their jobs-

-and this figure should be added to the
500,000	young people who are now jobless.
Meanwhile, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) was travelling across the country and telling people: Do not worry, things are going to change! What change, Mr. Speaker? She announced her much touted program with a two-month delay, supposedly for the sake of consultation. However, looking at each aspect of this program, we must conclude that she probably used those two months to fight her Cabinet colleagues who did not want to give her the funding. After all, she said she spent those two months on consultation.
However, representatives of the Canadian Federation of Students who were with the Minister on the platform when she made her announcement-and they are certainly by far the most representative of young Canadian students-told the media a few minutes later: We were never ever consulted about the program she just announced.
An important aspect of that program was municipal involvement. Here again, the Minister supposedly took two months to consult. I got in touch with the Canadian Federation of Municipalities, Mr. Speaker, and this is the answer I was given: We were never consulted at all. This despite the fact that the Minister was talking enthusiastically about a new consensus as a result of consultation. When I put the question to her in the House, she had the nerve to say she had consulted with the Mayor of Gander. My colleague from Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) called the Gander Municipal Council and said: Is it true that the Minister of Employment and Immigration called you and you said that municipal involvement in Challenge '85 was the answer to your prayers? What he answered was quite the contrary, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration is really trying to pull the wool over the eyes of the Canadian public. She would have our young people believe that this summer the outlook will be very encouraging for them. The fact of the matter is that the statistics we saw today, and I take the Member for Champlain (Mrs. Champagne) as my witness, I will bet anything, Mr. Speaker, that we "ain't seen nothing yet", indicate that there will be a lot more young people unemployed next summer and that the Minister's program will be no help at all in dealing with the situation.
Mr. Speaker, private sector involvement was also touted as a broad consensus, and the rest. The Minister of Employment and Immigration said at her press conference: I met with seven or eight big wheels who promised us 10,000 jobs. The next day, representatives of these big corporations said: We never guaranteed her 10,000 jobs. Mr. Speaker, we now see that on three counts the Minister of Employment and Immigration has not been clear, straightforward or accurate. And this has not met with any opposition from their backbenchers.
This summer, when young people in their ridings come to see them, the municipalities will have to tell them they do not have an extra 25 per cent nor an extra 15 per cent to spend on social benefits, because the Minister got her program out too late ... In Quebec, all municipal budgets have been voted on; they could not know that the Minister of Employment and Immigration would impose a surcharge of 25 per cent for labour plus 15 per cent for social benefits and another 20 per cent for miscellaneous expenses.
I know that there are former mayors here, the Hon. Member for Champlain happens to be one of them. I am sure he was a good mayor and that he knows what a municipal budget is. He had a sharp pencil in those days and I suspect every cent was accounted for in his budgets. That is why he too knows what is going to happen. Most municipalities have already-produced their budget, so they are not likely to be in a position to do much to create jobs for young people. I hope he will take the floor later on to urge that such expenditures be fully paid so as to relieve the small municipalities in our ridings. It is all very well to say that the private sector will take over but, Mr. Speaker, there are some 32 municipalities in my riding, including one with a service station and a corner store, so where is the private business that will hire young people this summer, Mr. Speaker? It is the same thing in all ridings- municipalities made up mostly of farmers. The private sector is simply not prepared to hire students.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration announced another initiative, the fall stage of Canada Works, but here we are in the middle of winter and there again, she was not clear, concise and definite.
Mr. Speaker, you will notice one thing about your allocation which is supposed to be more generous than or at least equal to

that of your predecessor: the Minister of Employment and Immigration conveniently forgot to tell you that it has to be spread out over two years instead of only one, so you can imagine what will happen next year! The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) says the same thing. You will have the surprise of your life, because the Minister of Employment and Immigration expects that money to last for two years. That is what her budget provides, Mr. Speaker; it covers two fiscal years. I am certain that our honourable colleagues will have to eat humble pie when they realize next year that the Minister of Employment and Immigration, instead of giving them the same budget as before, will give them in fact only half of it and say: "I am sorry, but you used all of it the first year, too bad!" But we shall watch her closely. If the Conservatives do not, you can rely on us, Mr. Speaker. We shall watch her because we know that she is trying to hide the truth from the unemployed, but the figures speak for themselves. There used to be all kinds of programs. We are now being told to forget about those programs because the private sector will take over. As far as private investments are concerned, it seems that up to now, our money was flowing to the States. Now foreign investments will solve our problems.
The Government destroyed FIRA. The Prime Minister went to New York on his hands and knees to make certain that the Americans would say: "We finally have a flunkey in Canada." What did we get? Except for the fact that the Prime Minister lost his dignity, what did the people in Champlain, the people in Beauharnois and the people in Shefford get? Mr. Speaker, here is what they got, absolutely nothing for now! Private investment in Canada has not increased, contrary to what the Prime Minister had forecast. Even worse, we have a serious unemployment problem. Yet, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, who should show some understanding and compassion for the unemployed, not only is not helping them to find jobs, but has also decided to reduce their unemployment benefits. She is now hiring a special team, which is being called the "Flora Hit Squad", to try and persecute the poor unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, we can see what is going on in our constituencies. All the Members, especially those whose unemployment offices come under the Longueuil Data Processing Center, are well aware of what is now happening to a great number of unemployed.
I am convinced that, every week, in their riding offices, my colleagues see a good many unemployed workers who complain that they are still waiting for their cheques, that they have

I know such cases and so do my colleagues. But what is the Minister of Employment and Immigration doing? Eliminating jobs instead of improving services. That has me deeply worried because not only has the Government failed to keep its promise to create jobs, but they are treating unemployed people like dirt. It is on that particular point that our colleagues opposite should urge the Minister of Employment and Immigration to give an account of herself.
We have heard of typical cases of proceedings taken against various people, more evidence of the fact that they are openly insensitive towards men and women who have precious little. In the course of the coming weeks, I intend to ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration to stop prosecuting the unemployed and persecuting poor people. I will take my hat off to her if she can find jobs for them, but that is a far cry from reality.
After seeing some of the elements of the summer program, Mr. Speaker, 1 am prepared to predict that her program will be a flop. I can tell you that it will not work out at the municipal level because most municipalities have already voted on their budget. I can tell you that the private sector program will not lead to a fair distribution of funds, particularly in the Province of Quebec, because cities and towns will take the lion's share to the detriment of rural communities. Since the allocations are not based on distribution by riding, there will not be fair and equitable distribution to take regional unemployment into account, and that has me worried.
Mr. Speaker, I am not interested in partisan politics, but I do want to make sure that the people . . . there is the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin) laughing his head off, he knows very little besides partisan politics, of course, but we are used to that kind of attitude. Member for Charlevoix: instead of laughing at the unemployed as he is now doing in the House, he should see to it that the jobless in his riding are properly treated, that they get their cheques on time, that UIC public servants treat them as people who have paid their premiums. Take the floor, say what you think, tell everybody what your constituents think. That is what counts. That is why you were elected to Parliament, not to crawl on your

knees before the Cabinet. There may be an opening, but there are too many of you for that one job. That is not what you came here for, you have to speak up for your constituents.
Let us talk about those who claimed to have the ultimate solutions to the problems of unemployment. I am sure the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Vincent) promised during the election campaign that he would find new jobs for textile workers. Mr. Speaker, a lot could be said about the commitments that were made. And also a lot about the promises that were broken, Mr. Speaker.
Most of them!
most of them, and probably the only promise the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has honoured-
The uniforms!

-there was the promise of new uniforms. On that point, takers beware! There was also the promise to appoint friends. The Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne) says: As we had done. Mr. Speaker, all this goes to say that I am surely disappointed with this Government's performance, disappointed with their lack of imagination, and the realization that this Government which had answers to all the problems has managed to make problems worse, instead of finding solutions. And we have seen them in action for some months already. speechtext:
I want to make a comment, Mr. Speaker. I can understand my honourable colleague being disappointed. He is disappointed because he says that this will not work next summer. There is no reason why it should not. My honourable colleague is right to say that the municipal budgets have been approved. It is true that the municipal budgets have been approved, and most of them provide for premiums or hiring programs for next summer. Municipalities have always done this. It is not the first time.
The Hon. Member should at least recognize that we keep our promises. What we had promised was some participation, but we said that we would place more emphasis on the private sector. We should give the private sector a chance to prove itself next summer. We have no reason not to. You have developped an insatiable society. Last year, you approved special budgets for church roofs, judo schools, and so on. You have created such appetites that, today, no repairs are made to city halls, community halls or church roofs without an application for assistance being submitted to the Federal Government.
You have built a society in which people say: Everything must be kept as it was in the past. From now on, tomorrow is like yesterday indexed. This is impossible. Let us give new ideas and new programs a chance to prove themselves. The private sector will join in and so will the municipalities and the community sector. There is not much difference as far as the community level is concerned. If we give a chance to this program, we shall see that it can work quite well.

I am very glad to have heard the comments of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Hudon). He has learned his lesson well. However, Mr. Speaker, if he is convinced he is right, why has the Minister for Employment and Immigration mentioned a commitment for 10,000 jobs? Something different was said the
February 12, 1985

next day. Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary is not doing justice to his Minister. She also said that she had consulted the municipalities. We can see that it is not true. She said that she had consulted the young people. She called in three or four young Conservatives. Is this what you call nationwide consultation? The Parliamentary Secretary, who certainly has a lot of potential, should widen his Field of vision if he wants to replace his Minister one day. He should have more imagination than she does, because she has not achieved much since her appointment, unfortunately. As for me, Mr. Speaker, 1 am sure that if a fellow like him stops learning his lessons by heart and reading the releases of his Minister and shows some imagination, he could eventually get noticed by the Prime Minister. However, if he continues to act in this way and to protect the Government like he is now doing, neither his constituents nor the Prime Minister will appreciate him.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment of course on the marvelous speech made by the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre). Several times now, the numerous new Progressive Conservative members have been referred to as back-benchers. I would rather be ... I would like to say to the Hon. Member for Shefford that, even if I sit on the front benches, 1 would rather be a good back-bencher than a former half-minister. For the information of the Hon. Member for Shefford, I have taken stock of our investments in the Charlevoix riding and they now reach over $5.5 million. I am very proud of that since it is far better than anything ever achieved by my predecessor, who was a senior minister in his government.

It was the same under my predecessor who held some important portfolios in the former government but who could not, as he admitted himself, find any cure-all. Mr. Speaker, I would like to take part in the debate on the motion which has been placed before the House by the Hon. Member for Kam-loops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). It states:
That this House commends the Government of Manitoba for its positive policies of job creation which have produced the lowest unemployment level in Canada, and calls upon the Government to adopt a similar course of economic expansion-
I will speak against the motion because of my history in Manitoba. Before I do that, however, I would like to take exception to what the Hon. Member said about Manitoba. He said that it was a have-not province. As far as I am concerned, Manitoba is not a have-not province. I am very proud to be a Manitoban, and particularly proud to represent a Manitoba seat in Parliament. I take exception to his calling Manitoba a have-not province. If he is referring to the fact that we are one of the five provinces which qualify for equalization payments, I would possibly accept that. But to call Manitoba a have-not province is not correct.
I sat in opposition in the provincial Legislature for four years during the time of the Ed Schreyer Government. I also sat in the Sterling Lyon Government as a government Member. I think that regardless of what government is in power-whether it is Liberal, NDP or Conservative-they are all concerned about unemployment. No one likes to see students, youth or others in this country unemployed. I want to make it clear that we are not condemning the NDP Government of Manitoba for trying to create employment. However, I would suggest that I do not agree with that Government's approach. Later on in the debate, I will cite some of the statistics about which the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) questioned the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) this morning.
The motion before us contains two questions. One of those questions is: What is the right approach? Is it that Government should provide all the jobs and that Government should become bigger and bigger? Or do we take the approach which the Conservative Government believes is correct and put the finances of the Government into shape in order to create an economic confidence in the country so as to bring private investment back to create the long-term jobs which we are looking for at the present time?
What the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap said is not new to me. I heard it many time when I was in the provincial Legislature in Manitoba. We are talking about the different
philosophies of two Parties. The NDP believes that we should have bigger and bigger government, which would create jobs and have more government-owned companies. That is not surprising. One of my colleagues in the provincial Legislature-I believe it was the Hon. Member for Morris-had a copy of the Regina Manifesto, which was the philosophy of the CCF Party when it was founded in 1934. When I hear NDP Members stand up in this House and in the provincial House, I reflect back to many of the resolutions which were in that Manifesto. It called for more government involvement, ownership and spending of taxpayers' money. Therefore, it is not surprising to me that NDP Members in this House talk against the Investment Canada Bill. Neither is it surprising that they support more government spending to create more jobs. That philosophy is not particularly agreeable to me, otherwise I would be sitting with those gentlemen. I think the correct approach to this problem would be to let the free enterprise system have the initiative, interest and confidence to go ahead with its work in our economy.
This morning the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap said that the Manitoba Government had created approximately 20,000 new jobs in 1983, and that in the First half of 1984 it created another 10,000 jobs. I felt it incumbent upon me to call Statistics Canada to obtain job figures for the past few years. I looked at the yearly average of those statistics. In other words, the yearly average of employment in StatsCan figures takes into account the valleys and the peaks, month by month, for a particular year, whether it be for employment, unemployment or the labour force. When the Conservative Government in Manitoba assumed power in 1977, there were
423.000	employed people in Manitoba. Those people were employed either by Governments, federal, provincial and municipal, or by private enterprise. When the Government left office in 1981, four years later, there were 453,000 people employed. StatsCan figures indicated that we had created
30.000	new jobs. I cannot agree with the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap because the Statistics Canada figures show that in 1982 there were 442,000 people employed, in 1983 it was 461,000 and in 1984 it was 465,000. So that the total increase in jobs over the last three years under the New Democratic Government in Manitoba amounts to 12,000 new jobs. Now where are all the jobs that Party is claiming are out there? In actual fact, if the Hon. Member wants to check this month's Statistics Canada report, he will find that the actual number of employed people in Manitoba for January, 1985 was 460,000.
What does this mean, Mr. Speaker? We have a Government in Manitoba which is taking the same basic approach as did the former Liberal Government. It is taking the approach of spend, spend, hire the people under government programs and leave the free enterprise system where it is. It is the kind of "We don't need free enterprise" approach. Yet that Government has created only something like 12,000 new jobs according to Statistics Canada. In 1981, when the New Democratic Government took over, the figure was 453,000. In 1984 it is

465,000.	Yet the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap is claiming there were 21,000 new jobs created last year in 1983 and another 10,000 jobs in the first half of 1984. Somewhere someone is a little mixed up.
What these figures make very clear, Mr. Speaker, is that the government approach in Manitoba is for short-term jobs. The average statistics take into consideration the peaks and valleys, but at the end of the year the question is: At how many new jobs have we actually averaged out? That is why our Government does not believe in that kind of approach. We are looking for long-term jobs, not short-term jobs, which will perhaps qualify a person for unemployment insurance benefits after he or she has put in a period of part-time work. I have talked to the young people in my constituency, Mr. Speaker, and they have told me that they want a job which they know will be there a year from now. They do not like this idea of taking a job for six weeks or 12 weeks and not knowing whether, after the three months is over, they will have a job or whether they will have to go on unemployment insurance. They want longterm jobs.
I have an excerpt from the Winnipeg Free Press of May 12, 1984. I know I am not supposed to say this, but I wish some of the Liberals were in the House at this time because it pertains to the activities of the Liberal Party in Manitoba. It relates to how the Liberal Party in Manitoba tapped into the work job program. The article states that it was hoped that the job program would not be political, but the Liberal Party seemed to have tapped into it and it actually helps pay for office help in the provincial Liberal Party's office. I do not believe that these are the kinds of jobs we are looking for. We are looking for long-term jobs which are created by private enterprise.
I was advised that one of the priorities of the Manitoba Highways Department was to put up the job program signs. We have these all over Manitoba. They are white and green. They advertise how good the job program is in Manitoba. I do not think that that is the kind of jobs we are looking for, where the priority is putting up signs. We are looking for long-term programs.
If this program is so good, why did Manitoba have the slowest rate of employment growth of all the provinces between December, 1983 and December, 1984? That statistic is right out of Statistics Canada. It had the slowest rate of growth of employment compared to all other provinces. That Government has taken the same approach as the former Liberal Government, and obviously it is not working, Sir.
The other thing that is wrong with the Manitoba job fund is that it perpetuates the notion that the best way to create jobs is for Government to give someone the money to go out and hire someone. That does not work, Sir. There has to be a reason in the first place to hire someone other than that you receive x number of dollars from a level of Government. It does not matter how many dollars you have, there is not enough job fund money to spend in order to get those 40,000 people who are unemployed in Manitoba working again. We need that free enterprise system which acts as the engine of growth in our economy.

The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North asked this morning about the deficit. I believe, if I remember correctly, he said to my colleague that the former Conservative Government had deficits as well. I would like, through you, Mr. Speaker, to advise the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North that the Conservatives took over part way through 1977, in October of 1977, and at the end of that fiscal year there was a deficit of $191.3 million. When we took over at that time it was projected to be $270 million, but we were able to cut it back to $191 million in the first six months of our term. We will take credit for the following four years. Then, from 1978 to 1979 there was a $84.3 million deficit. In 1979-1980 there was a $44.3 million deficit. We will take credit for the last half of 1982. When we changed Governments in the fall, the deficit was $251 million. That makes a total of $429 million of deficit accumulated in four years under our Progressive Conservative Government.
I would like to advise the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre that in 1982-1983, under the New Democratic Government, there was a $435 million deficit. In 1983-1984 there was a $426.7 million deficit and in 1984-1985 it has been estimated that the deficit will be in the order of $488.7 million, for a total of $1,350 billion of accumulated deficit in three years. The Province of Manitoba in its first 112 years of operation accumulated a deficit of $1,344 billion. It has taken the new NDP Government in Manitoba just over three years to double that figure. Now in Manitoba, a family of four is looking at something like $619 per year in taxes just to cover the interest, Sir. Yet, even with all of that spending, which is the philosophy of the former Liberal Government and the present NDP Government in Manitoba, what are the employment statistics?
Employment in Manitoba in December of 1984 increased by only .9 per cent-that is less than 1 per cent-while in the rest of Canada, employment increased by 2.4 per cent. That tells me something, Mr. Speaker. It tells me that the rest of Canada believes that what the Conservative Government of Canada is doing is correct. But in our own Province of Manitoba, which is still under the influence of the NDP Government and its philosophy of "spend, spend, spend", employment has only increased by less than 1 per cent.
The NDP Government has done a number of things that I believe are discouraging economic expansion by the private sector. First, it introduced the one-and-a-half per cent payroll tax, which is a disincentive for people to hire in the first place, or even to create new jobs. The other thing which has happened is that under the NDP Government in Manitoba, spending by that Government has increased by 42 per cent while the economy has only grown by 24 per cent. Spending has outpaced the economic growth by some 18 per cent. The annual manufacturing investment, Mr. Speaker, has fallen off by 19.9 per cent over the last three years. Yet those Hon. Members talk about increased investment in our province. The NDP administration has gone even further. It has increased the sales tax to 6 per cent from 5 per cent. Hydro rates have increased by 22 per cent over the past three years. I was proud to be part of a Government which never increased taxes. We actually

I think it is very clear, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada do not want to see that happen again. They got rid of a Liberal Government which thought the answer was to spend, that money could cure all. The only firm basis for economic recovery is a restoration of confidence. A confident private sector will act to create jobs without the need of government interference and control. I hope that the Government is right, Mr. Speaker, but on the basis of past experience, with all the attempts of the former Liberal Government by way of tax concessions, tax write-offs, grants and loans, the private sector did not pick up the slack. I would like to say a few words about the speech of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker). He suggested again and again that our Party is opposed to the private sector and that we believe the Government should do more and more. There is no truth in that, Mr. Speaker. The Member talked about the Regina Manifesto. Of course the Regina Manifesto talked about a great deal of public ownership because when it was drafted in 1933 the free enterprise system, as we knew it then, was dead in the water. I believe it would not be far wrong to say that 25 per cent or more of the people of Canada were unemployed at that time. The members of the CCF were not the only people who said that the free enterprise system was dead at that time. That was 50 years ago and a great deal has happened since. I am surprised at the Member for Winnipeg-St. James because he has not even studied the situation in Manitoba. Manitoba has a publicly owned telephone system. I was not extablished by some wild-eyed radical socialist. It was established in 1907 by a Conservative Government. The Premier at that time was Sir Rodney Roblin, who is the grandfather of the present Leader of the Conservative Party in the other Chamber. Manitoba has a publicly owned hydro electric system which was established by Liberal Governments. Nine of the ten provinces in Canada have publicly owned hydro electric systems. There has been no more successful a hydro electric system that that of the Province of Ontario. That publicly owned system was established by a Conservative Government . The Province of Ontario has had a Conservative Government for the last 40 years.
Hear, hear!

Hon. Members applaud, Mr. Speaker. I ask them why a Conservative Government, which believes in a free enterprise system, continues to have a publicly owned system. It is because it is obvious that the publicly owned power system operates more effeciently and cheaply than would a private system. That is all that we have said and all that we will continue to say. There are certain fields in which a publicly owned operation is more efficient and brings more benefit to people than a private system would.
The Government of Manitoba has decided that if it must choose between putting people to work and having a larger deficit, or cutting back on the deficit and having more people unemployed, it prefers to have a large deficit. The Government of Manitoba has spent over $200 million on jobs programs. Of course some of those jobs are temporary. However, I suggest to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James that a temporary job is better than no job at all. The Government of Manitoba did not just throw money away. It has tried to develop projects in co-operation with municipalities and the private sector. Many of those jobs are temporary, but many of them have led or will lead to permanent jobs.
Look at the situation we are in, Mr. Speaker. We have 1.5 million unemployed. Last month there were 507,000 young people between the ages of 15 and 24 unemployed. I have been here longer than most Members and I remember when the rate of unemployment was much lower than it is now. Experts at the Economic Council and in the universities told us that the problem was that people had not been trained to fill the available jobs. We have never made greater efforts to train people, Mr. Speaker. We have never spent more money on education. We have developed our high school system. We have vocational schools and community colleges. Our universities are training people in fields for which they think there will be employment opportunities. Over one-half a million of our young peole are unemployed. That is a disgrace, and I suggest that we will have a lost generation because they will eventually give up looking for jobs.

Not only must we reduce unemployment to a level comparable to those in countries such as Japan and Germany, but we must concentrate on those groups in our society which cannot find employment even when times are good and the unemployment rate is half of what it is now. I am talking about the handicapped people, hardly any of whom work. Many are working in sheltered work shops at much below the minimum wage.
