Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to enter into debate this afternoon on the motion introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). I have listened to the debates in this House today. Very often these kinds of debates are philosophical. I think it important that this House of Commons, the House of representatives of the men and women of Canada, should spend time discussing and debating and having a discourse on the various philosophies of how economic and social development can occur.
We see in the Province of Manitoba an alternative model of development, different from what exists in all the other provinces, and certainly different from the policies and programs of our present federal Government. It is a policy based on the notion and the philosophy that there is a legitimate role of government, that government has a role to play in the economic well-being of the country. It is not just a passive role, Mr. Speaker. Government has a responsibility to play an active role in determining the well-being of our economy.
Many of our friends across the way would disagree with that. Many believe that what government does is necessarily wasteful, unproductive and an impediment toward sound economic recovery. If only we can clear government out of the way and allow the private system to do its thing, so to speak, then economic prosperity would descend upon all of us and it will be fine, thank you very much.
I think that is a relatively simplistic notion. It is a reactive, regressive notion. It is a notion that has been tried in the past and shown not to work. We are living in a society today that is very centralized and interdependent, one that depends upon a well functioning, efficient and active government, but for a government to sit back and allow the forces of the marketplace to determine the economic well-being, I think is foolish and will not work.
When we hear from our Conservative friends-and we heard this message from our Liberal friends when they were in government-that private enterprise must be a major vehicle for economic recovery, I am dismayed. We look at our present economic situation and we know we have had free enterprise government in this country since it was founded. We know we have the so-called free enterprise governments in nine of our provinces, and yet we are dealing with record high levels of unemployment and economic hardship. These same people say,
"We have too much government and that is why we have these problems", but they are the ones who have been in power all this time. If there is any blame, surely the Tory and Liberal Governments have to be blamed because they have been in charge of our economy together with the captains of industry and finance who have made the economic decisions for us. Surely they are the ones we have to blame for record high levels of unemployment, for the deficits and for the economic mess in which we find ourselves.
Let there be no doubt about it; we are in an economic mess. Our country has a wealth of resources and a sparse population. We are young and much needs to be done. For us to end up with massive deficits and record high levels of unemployment surely leads any reasonable man or woman to say that something is wrong. Surely we have to blame the people who have been in charge of the economic destiny of the country, namely, large financial and industrial institutions as well as Liberal and Tory Governments. Their economic model has not worked and is not working.
In the Province of Manitoba there is another economic model which believes that people come first and disagrees with the comments which I heard just a few minutes ago made by the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) who was concerned about the crumbling of the major financial pillars of the country. We are concerned about the financial pillars, but our first concern is the human pillars of the country. We are concerned because there are men and women who do not have enough food to put on their tables every night. We are concerned because thre are men and women who line up every day waiting for a bowl of soup or a sandwich, and that is their only sustenance. We are concerned about the pillar of basic human decency-people having the right to food and a secure roof over their heads. This is why the Government of Manitoba has put people first. If it means a deficit, unfortunately it means a deficit. However, it would rather have a deficit than large numbers of people declaring personal bankruptcy or large numbers of people going without a decent meal. I suppose it is a difference in priorities. There is no doubt, from the comments of Conservative speakers, that their priority is the financial pillar of the country. Our priority is the human pillar, as I said. We would rather have a deficit than see people starve. That is our priority, and that is the priority of the Government of Manitoba.
It is important to have alternatives, living as we do in a day and age of very rapid economic and social changes. I would be the first to admit that no one has a blueprint, no one has all the solutions. We are dealing with economic and social situations with which societies in the past have not had to deal. We are dealing with a technology which is rapidly expanding and wiping out jobs all over the place. Perhaps this means that the traditional notion of work and life's goals have to change. The traditional lifestyle of working five days a week for 30 or 40 years in pursuit of a career, retiring with a gold watch and in many cases dying of a heart attack after retirement, the traditional lifestyle which sustained our parents, grandparents
February 12, 1985

and great-grandparents, was important in the development of the country. Perhaps much of it is no longer applicable, given the newer technologies and the types of changes that are being introduced in society. The whole notion of work and how men and women acquire income will have to be changed as we go into the 21st century.
New problems face governments and the men and women who represent their fellow citizens. There are difficult decisions to be made. There is no doubt that we are in a crisis, that there are tremendously large deficit and that the cost of servicing them are extremely high. While recognizing that, 1 wish members of the Conservative Party would also recognize the tremendous difficulties faced by ordinary men and women in their lives. I wish they would also show the same concern about starvation and malnutrition in this country as they show about deficits and the cost of servicing them. Surely honourable men and women would place people before deficits and financial statements in their list of priorities. I expect members of the Conservative Party to place to welfare of their fellow citizens before deficits, the largeness of them and the cost of servicing them.
Let me return to the point I was trying to make. There are no easy solutions. There are no blueprints, so to speak. All we know is the general directions in which society must go in order for us to begin to find some of the possible solutions to the economic, social and cultural problems we face in this day and age. One of the directions is surely one of co-operation. The different sectors in society-business, labour and government-must learn how to co-opperate. The days of confrontation must be over. There has to be give and take. This means that government is involved as an active partner, not a passive one. Many Conservative colleagues would attempt to suggest that government's role is to get the heck out of there and leave it up to the private sector. That type of thinking is old thinking and will not help us to attain the solutions we need. We must accept the fact that government has a role to play.
Why?

I hear the Hon. Member for Crowfoot. It is sad when men and women who put themselves forward to govern do not even know why they should govern. Indeed I find it sad. If they do not know why they should be governing, they should get out of there and let people govern who know why they should be governing. If the Hon. Member for Crowfoot does not have the role of government in his head yet, I am afraid we are in a sadder situation than I previously thought. Maybe that is the reason the Hon. Member is not in Cabinet. I hope at least the cabinet Ministers know why they are governing and the role which government has to play.
There is no denying that in this day and age, in this very complex period in the history of the human race, government has an essential function to play. If the Hon. Member for Crowfoot and some of his colleagues do not understand that, indeed it is a sad day.
I could go on enumerating the many reasons we need government. I should like to give one simple example which is
Supply
occurring back home with Pioneer Trust. Some of our Conservative colleagues believe that government should not be involved, that it should get out of it, that it should not even regulate trust industries. If that were to occur, we would see bandits in the field and people losing their deposits. People in Regina right now are losing their deposits and life savings, retired businessmen and farmers who sold their land and do not have any pensions but have $100,000 or $120,000 in Pioneer Trust. All at once they are discovering that half of their life savings have been wiped away because of the great engines of free enterprise.
They think the Government shouldn't do anything.

On top of that, they believe that the Government should not do anything. These people are really crazy. It is scary and frightening, though it is understandable in some ways. When a society goes through very rapid change as we have over the past few decades, a reaction sets in. People become afraid of change. They seek some stability. They seek a way to return to the way things were before. We find attempts to return to the times of Doris Day, Dwight D. Eisenhower and apple pie. Just wishing that to happen will not make it happen. In fact, it is quite impossible to turn back the clock.
As these Hon. Members attempt to grapple with contemporary problems, I hope they realize that returning to the simple days of the 1940s and 1950s will not happen. I hope they will smarten up and begin to realize that they are living in the contemporary world, and I hope that they will begin to offer some contemporary solutions and introduce some contemporary thinking.
I am sure that it will take a while for that to happen to the Hon. Member for Crowfoot and to some of his colleagues. After all, he comes from dinosaur country, and the ghosts of the dinosaurs still wander about those lonely and bleak plains. We can understand that. However, I certainly hope that other Members, and particularly cabinet Ministers, will begin to realize why they are in Government. I hope they will begin to realize what their function is and to know the job they are supposed to do.
To return to the point I was making earlier, for us to begin to develop and evolve solutions to these contemporary problems, we need a co-operative model. We need co-operation between business, labour and government. We need to understand the important role that government also must play in the arrangement of things. We have to understand and appreciate as well the role that labour must play. We also have to appreciate the role that capital and business must play. However, we have seen that the new right-wing Tory solution is that Government should decrease its function, that labour should reduce its demands and its wages, and that-

Right on.

February 12, 1985
Supply

An Hon. Member said, right on. The Tory solution means that we should give greater benefits to the private sector and then somehow or other development and jobs will appear.
I am reminded of a statement made by the Alberta Minister of Employment who said at the beginning of the summer that unemployment was good because it kept wages down and it kept the workers more productive. It kept the workers frightened of losing their jobs and so they were less likely to make new demands.
In these hard economic times, we see that working people are supposed to lower their expectations. We find that people on unemployment insurance, pensioners or people on welfare are to expect less, that the people who are the captains of industry and finance are supposed to get more wealth, and that this in turn will somehow generate jobs.
Government members never talk about the responsibilities of capital. Has the Government ever asked the investment industry in the country to keep its money in Canada? No. The Hon. Member for Crowfoot criticized the National Energy Program. I as well criticized the National Energy Program and I too voted against it, though I suspect for different reasons from those of the Hon. Member for Crowfoot. I remember reading in the financial pages of The Globe and Mail that the oil industry in the country had a pretty good year last year. In fact, it had one of its record profit years. Companies like Exxon in the United States were not having all that great a year, but the oil companies in Canada were having a good year.
Up 50 per cent.
Up 50 per cent. That is not bad. Is that money staying in this country?
Yes.

Now we hear the Hon. Member for Crowfoot saying, yes. A few moments ago, he said that the National Energy Program was driving investment out of the country. Now he is saying that those profits are staying in the country. I would suggest that a great many of those profits are leaving this country.
International capital has no loyalty to any particular country. International capital is not loyal to this country even though its profits are made from the resources of this country. Much of that money will be laundered through dummy companies in the Bahamas so taxes will not be paid on it, and then it will get reinvested in other places. Hon. Members says that that is just smart accountaing practices. Of course, if one is in charge of an oil company, those are smart accounting practices. However, if Hon. Members suggest that smart accounting practices will create jobs for Canadian men and women, they are wrong. Indeed, they have their heads in the sand. Indeed, their prescription for the solution to the problems we are facing will create more disaster. Therefore, I believe we have put forward a good motion, a motion that lauds a
provincial Government that is attempting to develop a different program that offers different solutions, solutions based on the notion that people come first.

speechtext: Questions and comments?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure you are somewhat surprised that I would rise after that speech. However, I have noted the logic of the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). He is a person who would take the view that all ducks are good swimmers, Simon is a good swimmer and therefore Simon is a duck.
I listened to the Hon. Member's convoluted statement consisting of things that he threw up in the air that landed we know not where and that he claimed to be somehow logical, factual. Therefore, on the basis of what he has said, Canada should somehow accept that as a legitimate speech to be made in the House of commons. I could tell the Hon. Member that it was a testament as to why there are only about 30 members of the New Democratic Party.
The Hon. Member went on to say that we said that we did not need government after I had questioned him as to whether or not government could be as efficient in creating jobs as the private sector. He took that to mean that we felt that governments were bad. Surely he knows that the federal Government of Canada is Progressive Conservative and that six provincial Government are Progressive Conservative. Obviously it is not Party policy to believe that Government is no good. We are here; he is not.
The Hon. Member said that the new energy program must be good because the oil industry is expanding and growing. Of course it is growing. It is growing precisely because there is a Progressive Conservative Government in Canada. It was in the four previous years that the energy industry was chased into Venezuela, the United States, Australia and New Zealand, and not only the industry for the western sedimentary basin but for the industrial sector in Canada as well. Those jobs were chased out of Canada along with billions of dollars of investment capital.
The Hon. Member simply cannot say that the industry is making a comeback. I just came back from a meeting with IPAC. They are here today and investing today because there is an expectation of change in the direction of policy. Every time oil companies begin to drill new wells, there is a new sense of activity being felt. The Hon. Member for Regina East ought to know that because his province feels the impact when the oil industry begins to develop and grow.
When the Hon. Member says that the oil industry is up 50 per cent, he deludes himself. He knows very well that it is up 50 per cent following four of the most disastrous years in its history. He also knows that it is up 50 per cent because the industry believes that there will be a turnaround. I would ask him how he could possibly stand there and shout out these so-called facts and figures, which he knows do not really represent reality or truth, to try to make people believe that he is giving suggestions as to how Canada can get back to a solid
February 12, 1985

bottom line economically and be competitive in the international market.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has failed to convince me, and I believe many others as well, that his examples for development in the oil industry are what will solve our problems. I would suggest that part of the major reason there has been a downturn in the oil industry is that the price of oil has fallen on the world market. When he suggests-
Is it up or down?

You are sitting down and I am standing up, so keep it easy.
We hear the Hon. Member for Crowfoot suggest that the decline in the oil industry is because of the National Energy Program, and that with a Conservative Government that program will be scrapped and the oil giants will have increased confidence. "Increased confidence" is another key slogan. Listening to the Tories reminds me of the Moonies. They have key phrases which get them all excited. Certain buttons get pushed. It is like mind training, and one of the key phrases is "increased confidence". It is as though they had jars of increased confidence which they hand out and sniff. They say that because a Tory Government was elected, increased confidence is occurring and money will be reinvested in oil development.
I would suggest that if the price of oil on the international market decreases, we will not have the increased confidence which will fuel activity in the oil industry. The only way to get increased activity in the oil industry is for the Government to give it further tax breaks and incentives until it makes sense for the oil companies to continue the economic activity.
It will be interesting to see how the Tory Government changes the National Energy Program. I would suggest that many of the oil companies, despite the rhetoric, have been able to live with it and have come to like it. I believe we will see opposition from oil industry people to the changes which will be made to the National Energy Program. Then we will see the Hon. Member for Crowfoot eating crow.
So much of the rhetoric has been to blame all the economic ills in western Canada on the National Energy Program. Once this excuse disappears, what excuse will be left? At some stage Tories will have to look at themselves and begin to accept some responsibility for what is happening, rather than pulling out a scapegoat everytime they want to make a boisterous speech which is full of sound and fury.

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment and a question for the Hon. Member. I listened intently to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) who supported the motion which was presented by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shus-wap (Mr. Riis). There was a Manitoban and a British Columbian who supported the motion, and now we have a Member from Saskatchewan adding his glorification to the motion.

He said that it was a "good motion" and one which "lauded a provincial Government", but he forgot to address himself to the pith and substance of it, which commends the Government of Manitoba for its policies. Three westerners have lauded a motion which inferentially condemns every other province of Canada and the people of those provinces.
I would point out to the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) that in 1983-84 the Province of Nova Scotia had the highest rate of growth in Canada. That is quite an accomplishment for a small, disadvantaged province like Nova Scotia. The Government, the private sector and mainly the people of Nova Scotia caused that economy to grow. I think the people of Nova Scotia will resent the western clique in the New Democratic Party who are inferentially condemning the efforts of the people of Nova Scotia by way of lauding the Province of Manitoba for its policies. I think the same could be said of every province of Canada which has laboured diligently on behalf of its people to establish better economic conditions. It is a well known fact that if we praise one we can be guilty of condemning others. That is exactly what the NDP has done with this motion. I would like the Hon. Member for Regina East to answer that. What has he got to say that is good about the Province of Nova Scotia and the other provinces of Canada?
I would like to add one comment before he answers that question. I want him to know that the policies which gave rise to the economic superiority of Manitoba were policies established by Duff Roblin when he was Premier. He took the hard decision to establish hydro and other resources in that province, which fueled the growth in the Province of Manitoba. It has little, if anything, to do with the current Government of the Province of Manitoba.

Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to hear the Hon. Member, when talking about his home Province of Nova Scotia, mention that one of the important players was government. I salute him for being civilized and enlightened enough to recognize that government has a role to play. The Hon. Member has been here for some time and I think he does recognize that government has a role to play.
He also recognized that it was the Government of Mr. Roblin which helped to develop hydro and other resources in the Province of Manitoba. Again, he recognized that Government had a role to play. It was a Tory Government, and it knew it had to play an activist role, otherwise those resources would not have been developed. What frightens me is that other Members believe that Mr. Roblin was wrong, that the Government of Nova Scotia in helping to develop jobs is wrong, and that governments should not have a role to play. They believe that if we left private enterprise alone, it would solve all our problems, develop hydro, create jobs and so on. It is that simplistic notion that scares the daylights out of me.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue and Canada Post):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some very positive developments are taking place in the economy

February 12, 1985
Supply
and our Government, although the motion before the House today seems to ignore entirely what has been happening during the last few months. I would like to point out, for instance, that during the third quarter, our economic growth has been remarkable, as much as 7.6 per cent. Mortgage rates have dropped at least 2 per cent since we took up our mandate, and this only since September 4. Canada's trade surplus is at a record high. Last year, inflation was at its lowest level since 1971, which will improve our competitive position abroad.
When we were brought to power on September 4, Canadians were clearly saying they wanted a fresh start. They had looked at past measures and realized that they had not been terribly effective. They saw there was too much confrontation between administrations, too much confrontation between the private and the public sector, too much confrontation between the Federal Government and the provinces. Canadians realized it was time the Government was involved in developing the answers, but involved in a sensible way instead of compounding the problem as had been the case before.
The message on September 4, Mr. Speaker, was loud and clear. Our immediate response was the strategy for economic renewal announced last November.
Canadians must, however, understand that the Government cannot manage this country's economy alone, controlling every little detail. That is not its mandate, Mr. Speaker. Its mandate is to administer the country in such a way that the economy progresses, but without undue intervention.
The Government does not dominate the economy, Mr. Speaker. It is part of the economy, one element of a living organism. It is a set of institutions and bodies that are involved in the production and consumer activities we call economic life.
Every healthy organism depends on the equilibrium of its components. If one of these components starts to grow excessively, the excessive demands it makes will weaken the organism. The Government's role is to maintain a correct balance in the economy between public and private interests. It must manage its own affairs to the best of its ability. It must provide for proper planning and avoid being forced into an excessively high deficit like the one we have today. It should also provide the economy with a general framework of policies, programs and regulations that will promote economic growth and create as much employment as possible. That is why we were elected.
To illustrate the importance of this notion of equilibrium, let us take inflation as an example. For many years this has been the economy's number one problem. Although Canadians have made tremendous progress in controlling inflation, the federal Government's structural and financial policies did not play the role they should have played in this struggle. In some cases, they made the fight against inflation even more difficult. One of the basic differences in what the Mulroney Government is doing is its more balanced approach to economic policy, an approach in which monetary, financial and structural policies are all oriented in the same direction. The main goal of this
approach will be to sustain non-inflationary growth and to create jobs by bringing interest rates down as far as possible. This approach demands that Parliament reduce financial imbalances and correct a number of structural problems. That is the direction we started to take following last November's economic message, and it will guide our decisions in the future.
Last November, the theme was how to control and manage an ever-increasing deficit. We must continue to do so and do it carefully and sensibly. The nation cannot go on mortgaging its future and hope to sustain economic growth, as was the case before September 4, Mr. Speaker, which was what Canadians understood when they gave us a clear mandate.
The measures we have already taken, namely, the expenditure cuts and other initiatives announced in the economic message, should start having a positive effect on the deficit in the next fiscal year.
There are those who claim that wanting to manage the national debt is to be insensitive to people's needs. That is not true, Mr. Speaker. Canadians realize that only by putting our finances in order will we be able to avoid overwhelming problems for the people of Canada, problems that would bring about a rise in interest rates, loss of jobs and a drop in investment. The measures we have already taken are those that we think will benefit the majority of Canadians. The measures we will take in future will meet the same criterion, and that is this Government's primary concern.
The deficit is not the only obstacle, Mr. Speaker. We will also have to restructure Government policies, regulations and economic programs to allow the creative energies of Canadians to be exercised freely. We must give individuals and firms in the private sector enough room to manoeuvre and make it possible for them to use their creativity and talents as productively and profitably as possible for the economy of this country. That is the challenge for 1985. That is why we have started one of the most thorough public policy reviews Canada has ever known. Our goal is a complete restructuring of Government policy over the next few years that will make our economy productive and, especially, make it more competitive.
Productive businesses must grow and create jobs, and make rational long-term plans. We have experienced in Canada a succession of arbitrary changes that created uncertainty and undermined confidence, both at home and abroad, especially where our small businesses are concerned. It is obvious that the recent experience has been harmful. Yet the status quo is no more acceptable. We are introducing changes, but in a consistent, reasoned way, and this is why this Government is involved in so much consultation.
There are many areas where action is needed. For instance, our new competition policy scheme would promote confidence. Government legislation has to be updated so that the production, distribution and treatment of information and computerization may contribute to our economic growth to a greater extent. Other statutes and regulations that affect the operation of businesses in Canada must also be streamlined, and above all modernized, Mr. Speaker. As we know, we have statutes that should have been amended long ago, but the previous
February 12, 1985

Government did not attend to that. We also support a larger degree of flexibility and productivity in our economy, and the adaptation to modern technology.
Mr. Speaker, no one can contribute more to this renewal and to the providing of new opportunities than small businesses. While they have always been neglected, for a number of years already they have been creating most jobs in Canada. Not only that, they have the greatest job creation potential in new fields. If we really want to entrust our economic growth to the private sector, Mr. Speaker, we must ensure that the free enterprise spirit will be rewarded through and with the entrepreneur. The Government must do all it can to help the entrepreneur, and above all to promote entrepreneurship.
We have indicated that the Government could lead the way. It can create a favourable climate. Moreover, whatever measures the Government can take, cost nothing in many cases or almost nothing to the Public Treasury, but we should not delude ourselves about the implications of that process. We have set ourselves the task of establishing in the economy a better balance between the public and the private sectors. Within the new framework we are putting in place, Canadians will have to expect less from governments and more from the private sector.
One of the key areas in which the private sector can meet the challenge is that of investments. An increase in productive investments would benefit all segments of the economy. We must remember, Mr. Speaker, that investments result directly in job creation and production growth. Just as important, Mr. Speaker, investment decisions will have to be taken to cope with rapid technological changes and an evolving world market. We should support any future improvement in productivity and above all in competition, mainly in the private sector.
Canada does not hold its rightful place among industrialized nations. If we are to be truly competitive at the world level, if we are to really develop new markets, we have to go into research and development. An increased level of research and development requires a major effort for which the Government alone should not be relied upon. Canadian businesses must have the will to contribute to that effort.
Training and retraining are also essential ingredients of our economic growth. They do make it a lot easier for the business community to hire the qualified staff it needs to be competitive. Equally important, they help people be more flexible when facing an ever-changing market place or a new and different occupation. That has to be our national priority. Time has come for the private sector to wonder how it might play a more significant role so that training and upgrading will be tailored to its real needs.
Mr. Speaker, access to export markets is another major obstacle which stands between the business community and success. It is a major challenge as well, and if we manage to live up to it we will be able to create many jobs. However, we must be prepared to take the odd chance and be more dynamic on foreign markets, yet remain convinced that we can indeed be competitive. And the only way to be more competititive, Mr. Speaker, is to boost our productivity and modernize our
Supply
facilities. Mr. Speaker, none of that is possible unless we change our attitude and our work methods. It simply cannot be achieved overnight. Since September 4, the Opposition keeps repeating nothing has been done, nothing has been done. They were in office for twenty years. Earlier this afternoon, 1 heard the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) talk about administrative decisions taken by the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board, but he did not bother to say that the CIRB management was appointed by the Liberals, not by us, not by this Government. If the administrative decisions of the CIRB are not coming out fast enough for the Liberals, they should talk to the management, they put them there. There is no way they can be critical about what is going on right now. Besides, the Hon. Member ought to know that this board is not answerable to the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion.
When we were elected last fall, Mr. Speaker, we examined the economic outlook and realized that it was not very promising. So we decided to draft an economic development plan, a plan to improve the economic outlook and to set up new structures more conducive to the expansion of the private sector. What we had in mind was to make significant progress in key sectors such as trade, research, development and investment. We know that by taking action in all these areas, we shall finally be able to have a healthy economy. That is what Canadians have been hoping for since September 4.
International figures are already showing that Canada has now gone ahead of a few other industrialized countries as far as industrial competition and standard of living are concerned.
The figures have been favourable since September 4 and the economic achievements I have just mentioned are encouraging. They should restore confidence and raise the level of expectations in Canada. However, we should not become too confident. We cannot forget that everything is not perfect in our country. Our economy is still held back by excessively high real interest rates and by progress made in the United States. Too much of our recent economic growth is the result of our enormous trade surplus, and business investment remains weak. The situation of our resource industries is still very precarious. Finally, our enormous annual deficit and increasing national debt threaten our prospects for lasting economic development and job creation.
Mr. Speaker, this brief examination of the recent ups and downs of our economic performance reminds us that we must continue to make level-headed and realistic judgments about our performance and economic prospects. It remains that we can do much more and that we are progressing daily. Canada still has unlimited opportunities, and while the Opposition may believe that there is nothing to do, Mr. Speaker, there is, in fact, much to do and this Government is committed to do it.
The business community still shows great confidence in the Government elected on September 4 and in the commitment necessary for economic renewal. That is what some favourable

February 12, 1985
Supply
economic indicators are telling us. It is also what small businesses are saying. That is why foreign investors are more interested in Canada than before. As these new investments create job opportunities, Canadians will become less concerned about the future of their jobs, their family and their country. They will tend to consume more. This is why confidence is so important. I believe that we have every reason to be confident and optimistic. Obviously, if any country in the world has every chance to succeed, it is Canada. We should believe in the initiatives taken by the Government and support them. With the assistance of the private sector, private business and small businesses, with a special emphasis on entrepreneurship, and in spite of the motion of the New Democratic Party today, this is what we must do.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister have already made their views known in this regard and outlined exactly what will be the policy of this Government.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member on a very fine address. There is a point I have been wanting to clear up and I have not been able to be recognized until now. A number of speakers today, particularly in the opposition Parties, have been comparing the number of unemployed in the fall and winter with those in the spring and summer. We all know unemployment increases in the fall and winter in normal years. It is a normal procedure. To compare the number of jobs in the fall and winter with those in the spring and summer is like comparing apples with horses. There is just no comparison, and it creates the wrong impression entirely.
Would the Hon. Member agree that it is unfair to make this kind of comparison? It gives a false picture entirely, and I think all of us want to be accurate when we present a picture to the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that my honourable colleague is quite right. It is time to stop misleading the Canadian people into believing just about anything, as was done in the past. We know what Canada's economic conditions are and we know that certain things happen at the same time each year. Certain things occur in the fall, and others in the spring or in the summer. We know that. What the Hon. Member says is quite true. The Opposition always tries to show that
it is not the same, that it is different and that it was always better before. If such was the case, Mr. Speaker, I wonder why they are still there. I am in complete agreement with my hon. colleague.

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening with some interest to the debate this afternoon, and this is once again an opportunity for this House to discuss what is without question one of the most important and significant issues facing Canadians. That is why I would like to begin my remarks with a small plea to Members on both sides of the House to come at this issue without illusion, mythology or theology. We should try to demonstrate to the Canadian people that we are both learning from history and preparing for the future based on reality, not on fantasy.
I listened to the speech made by the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Vincent). He had some interesting prepared comments and statistics about what has happened and what has not happened. I want to address my remarks to him as a new Member and other new Members and say that I think it would be a mistake if we were simply to pretend nothing good happened in the past and all that is happening now is perfect. That is simply not the case.
I was intrigued by his comments about interest rates. Let us be honest, the interest rate policy is in large part dictated by what happens in money markets in the United States. The U.S. is the largest financial market in the world. It determines the international flow of money. It determines the level of interest rates which all countries pay. Therefore, any Canadian Government of whatever stripe is always forced into the position of having at least to respond and be sensitive to that fact. We are not an island unto ourselves.
What about Austria?

It is not possible for us to isolate ourselves from a country with which we share a 5,000 kilometre border, a country with which we conduct 70 per cent of our trade. Large parts of our commercial exchange are affected by what happens in the U.S. Don't kid yourselves by saying that somehow it is going to change simply because you are here. That is not the key. The question is what kind of response is to be made.
The Hon. Member and others have talked about how to control inflation. We were the ones who controlled inflation. It did not happen on September 4. The inflation rate was down to 4 per cent before then and went down to 3.5 per cent after then. It had nothing to do with the election. We had to take very tough and strong measures, some of which were very unpleasant, to bring the inflation rate down. I hope the Conservative Government will accept the responsibility of keeping it that way. Let us not forget history. Let us not be like some Soviet revisionist historian and wipe out the past. There is an old cliche which says that those who will not learn from the past are bound to repeat it. We must realize that
February 12, 1985

inflation is always a problem. We have to deal with the matter but we cannot deal with it through some theological answer.
I was interested to hear the Hon. Member talk about the way in which the Government is freeing up the forces of private enterprise and allowing more competition. Which Government brought in the major policy of deregulation? It was not the Conservative Government. A year ago the Liberal Government deregulated the airline industry and provided more competition. Conservative back-benchers had better ask some tough questions about the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) because he is stopping the program. He is putting the brakes on it. He is falling back into the trap of holding on to what the old vested interests had to say. Therefore, the airline industry is now getting a different set of signals. It was not the Conservatives who argued for the removal of excess regulations. It was the Liberal Government that did that.
That is an important truth, because the negotiations which we had with the provinces on deregulating the trucking industry have now been held up for six months. The agreement was on the table last September. The Conservative Government has stopped that agreement from going ahead. That agreement had been arrived at by all the nice words that Conservatives love to use: consultation, discussion, co-operation, and federal-provincial agreements. That had all been done. It was on the table and had been agreed upon. The Conservative Government stopped it. If Conservative Members are really concerned about that, they should do something about it. They should ask members of the Ministry why they are being trapped by functionaires and the old vested interests. The whole move to deregulation has been put on hold in the transportation industry. That is a very serious consequence because we were making progress. Without even examining the issue, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) said that they were not going to touch Air Canada. That issue was to have been discussed by way of public hearing in a House of Commons Transport Committee. The new Prime Minister of Canada put the stop to that. Why has the Prime Minister stopped that particular intervention?
My point is that government Members should not delude themselves.
We are not.

Oh yes you are. I have listened to what you have said. There is a rank air of illusion in this Chamber every time a Conservative back-bencher rises to his feet with prepared notes from the Department of Finance.
You were not here.

I don't see any economic Ministers here either. They are so concerned about job creation that they have not found time to come to the Chamber for this very important debate.

Mr. Speaker, in response to the point of order, it is obvious from observing who is in the Chamber at the present time that the Minister is not exactly committed to coming to grips with the issues which are being debated by Members of Parliament.
This is an important resolution because it does point to a very important model. I would like to talk about how growth can be created in the country. This is probably the most important issue that we face. What is the role of Government in that particular exercise? How do we begin to develop the intervention and activity which will help create growth in the private and public sectors?
Not by spending money like you did.

I am going to answer that. It is clear how his comment that the Hon. Member does not know what he is talking about. I am here to educate him, and I am quite happy to do that. That is what the debate is for.
I'm not the one who spent millions, Lloyd.

I will come to that. In 1980, the Province of Manitoba had been ravaged by the Sterling Lyon Government. We had the highest rate of unemployment and the lowest rate of growth. Because of the lack of provincial Government activity in that province, we had the lowest rate of growth in Canada. There was nothing going on. There was no capital construction, no investment in the schools, and no private investment going on. That was the reality of Manitoba in 1980. By 1984, we had the highest rate of growth in Canada and one of the lowest rates of unemployment. Something happened in those four years which created a difference. What happened was a prime example of full co-operation between the federal Government, the provincial Government, municipal Governments and the private sector. That is where the resolution goes wrong. It only points to one level of partnership. The fact is that there was a partnership of all the major sectors in that economy. There was a different kind of federal involvement that went back to the grass-roots at the community level to help make policy and provide federal investment. What was important about the Manitoba experiment is that it was not simply a transfer of funds. It was a direct active involvement in regional economic development.
I will give one example. The federal Government initiated the core area initiative because we recognized that one of the best ways to generate growth in that province was through the

February 12, 1985
Supply
City of Winnipeg, which represents the major economic engine in that province. The centre part of the city had been allowed to deteriorate. There was no investment going on and it was not an attractive area to which to bring private sector involvement. We proposed to the provincial and municipal Governments that we would each put up one-third of the funds to invest in incentives for private business, to provide for community redevelopment, and to provide for a major restructuring of the downtown area. Three levels of Government co-operated. We managed together. We sat down on a monthly basis with the Mayor of the City of Winnipeg, the provincial Minister and the regional Minister and talked about how we could join efforts to create development for the City of Winnipeg.
We are seeing the results now. Close to 50 new small businesses have started up in one warehouse district. This is not government intervention. They are new small businesses in the service sector, the manufacturing area, and the retail area. The Member for the Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gorm-ley) should go and look at that because an entire section of the city has been turned around. Private business, using the incentive grants, is sponsoring that.
We have also provided for close to 3,000 units of housing being either built or rehabilitated. That was the major source of private construction activity in that city. The Tories do not understand that kind of thing, but the private sector of Manitoba understands it because, for the first time, it was given the incentive to go back to work.
A third area of co-operation between the federal, provincial and municipal Governments was the provision of a major incentive for development in the north of Portage la Prairie. We put a package together to provide for capital infrastructure, a new investment, and then used that to attract major development into that area. The result has been that a major developer has announced that he will go into the northern part of Portage la Prairie to create 200,000 square feet of new commercial space. There are presently negotiations going on for another 300 or 400 units of needed rental housing.
That is co-operation as it should really happen. Government should not be afraid to work with the private sector or the provincial or municipal governments. They should work together to create growth.
The result in that area was that we were able to provide several thousand new jobs. Furthermore, not only was the actual core area initiative itself important, each level of Government could use it as a framework for development and be in a position to provide further investment to enhance and attract further activity.
Members have heard us in opposition complain mightily about the cancellation of a National Research Council Centre which was to be part of that downtown development program in Winnipeg. We complained about it because it was a way the federal Government could effectively help the Province of Manitoba acquire new capacity in high-tech research and development. The side benefit of that is that it was designed to
attract a number of new high-tech manufacturing industries to the City of Winnipeg.
There were four major companies that were prepared to locate in Winnipeg and establish technology-oriented activities. They have now put their plans on hold because the federal Government cancelled the project. That is why it is important that the Government at the federal level recognize that it has an important and positive impact as an investor in communities, working in conjunction with other levels of government.
That is why we strongly object to the present plans of the Minister of Regional and Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) simply to transfer the funding. This means that the federal Government is denying itself the ability to provide further federal investment of this kind. It is removing itself from the planning and development activities in that region. It no longer has the capacity to determine how federal investments, whether in research or scientific development, capital structure or airports, are able to add to a growth business.
Let me give another example from Manitoba of tri-level co-operation. It was the signing of a major transportation agreement. After sitting down with the provincial Governments and discussing what would be the primary form of economic development, it was recognized that the Province of Manitoba was a major centre of transportation. Many of the facilities had been allowed to deteriorate over the years. We signed an agreement amounting to over $200 million to restore totally the Port of Churchill, repair the railway lines, and bring to Winnipeg for the first time the development, research and manufacturing of light grain cars that would be utilized in the entire grain network in western Canada as well as on the Churchill line. The agreement also included the expansion of the airport system and research and development.
I suggest to Hon. Members, who think they know so much, that this was done in conjunction with the private sector: thirty of the top business people in Winnipeg, many of whom were Conservative bagmen, financiers and campaign managers-I can name them-and I know the Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker) knows who I am talking about. They told me that they wanted to provide new investment at the University of Manitoba in management studies because they believed that that is the way of the future. They asked if the federal Government would help them. We worked with associates of that faculty and designed a management study program, transportation research centre because we recognized that new research was the way of the future. That was done with the province, the private sector and the universities, with the federal Government involving itself directly in economic development at the local level while using its investment funds to provide opportunities for new training, new research and new products.
That is an important model to be followed. It is very important that the Government not get itself so wrapped up in its theology that government should not play such a role that it withdraws from those potential investment opportunities to help the regions of Canada grow.
February 12, 1985
What about the people who said no? They said no to you.
Oh no, they didn't.
You are still in a dream.
I am talking about reality. I am talking about hard jobs. I am also talking about a reality in which there are a lot of people in Manitoba saying, "My God, I wish the other guys were back".
Name one, Lloyd.

I presented a petition in the House which contained 1,000 names of people who are objecting to the activity of the Government of Canada selling the National Research Council Centre. That was done in one weekend. We do not need much more help than that. There are thousands more who believe the same thing.
The Conservative Government never came to Manitoba to say that it will cancel the National Research Council Centre or the research grants. It was campaigning on a lie. The Conservatives did not say that they were going to cut back on those kinds of federal investments. They did not have a mandate to do it, and that is why Canadians have a serious mistrust of the Government. They can no longer believe the Government.
Not only did it not have a mandate to change that, it is now betraying that trust and losing the opportunities to create in Manitoba the high level technology job development that we began three years ago.
This is where the NDP resolution is wrong. The NDP should not only be taking credit for the Manitoba Government. While important and positive advances have been made in Manitoba, it has happened because there were several players and several partners. For all the talk we have heard from federal Conservative Members and Ministers about cooperation, consultation, negotiation and agreement, the NDP should look at the model of Manitoba to see how it works and how it turned that province around. Manitoba had the lowest rate of growth and one of the highest unemployment rates, but now it has a high rate of growth and it had some opportunities until the present Government began ripping those agreements apart and not taking its activities there.
The people of Manitoba are asking what happened to that co-operation and openness with respect to $72 million of equalization payments. Where is the co-operation when every level of government in that province and the private sector have asked for the restoration of that national research centre? Where is the co-operation with respect to the investment in such things as new training facilities in new community colleges?
The Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres said that it is important to train people. Our Government put $1 billion into the training program in 1982. The Conservatives are not the first to think of this. Part of the $1 billion that we put into that
Supply
program was designed to provide direct transfers to the community colleges run by the provinces and to the private sector to develop new training facilities.
Today, there is no longer any money for that skills growth fund. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has not contributed any money to provide for the new CAD-CAM centres and high-tech development centres. The ability to give assistance to provincial governments, native bands, women's groups and community corporations in order to develop new training facilities has been cut off.
The Government says that it believes in the investment in our human resources. I say to the Government, invest in them. Why did it cut the program off and stop funding the skills growth fund which is designed to help those provinces and expand the community colleges in every province in the country?
I believe there are lessons to be learned from the Manitoba example. They are lessons on co-operation and on how to work with the province to provide economic development. In order to accomplish this, it is necessary to have a federal Government that wants to participate as a partner and wants to invest.
Therefore, I would like to move an amendment to the motion, seconded by the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith): The amended motion would read:
That this House commends the Government of Manitoba and the former Liberal Government for their positive policies of job creation which have produced the lowest unemployment level in Canada, and calls upon the Government to adopt a similar course of economic expansion rather than the discredited policies of tax increases and spending cuts which it has pursued to date and which are largely responsible for the latest unemployment statistics, which show an alarming increase of 167,000 unemployed between December, 1984, and January, 1985.

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief comment. I am very fortunate to represent the community of North Batt-leford, which is the birthplace of the Hon. Member for Win-nipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). Let me say that the people there are able to contain the sadness at the fact that he is now living in Winnipeg. While I do not want to attack another Member personally, I suggest that what we have just heard is not only a sad example but a shameful defence of the kind of obscene waste of taxpayers' money to which the people of Canada quite resolutely said no on September 4.
We have heard these lame theories of economic development. I think the people of this country, and certainly their representatives in the House, acknowledge that there is definitely a role for government. I do not believe that any Member of our Government would disagree that there is a role for government, provincial governments, labour and all people to work together to promote a healthy and vibrant economy. It is not the role of government to waste untold millions of dollars on so-called economic development, as this Member from Winnipeg so shamefully claims when he says that that in some sense is economic development. That is wasting the taxpayers' money by simply giving vast quantities of money to projects

that did not promote in the long run economic development and, what is more important, human dignity. I think perhaps this Member owes this House a clearer explanation of just what he did to this country in his capacity as the one who dispensed all of this money in the name of so-called economic development.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Eton. Member for the opportunity to elaborate even further on the very constructive developments that took place in the Province of Manitoba. I want to register on behalf of that province a serious objection to the language he used in calling it shameful. Those projects were not federal waste. They were done in consultation with the Chambers of Commerce of that Province, with the City of Winnipeg, the Province of Manitoba, and a wide variety of community organizations. The Hon. Member for The Batt-lefords-Meadow Lake has just in effect insulted thousands of people in Manitoba who worked together on those projects. We are used to that kind of arrogance on the part of the Conservatives.
Oh, oh!
Who is calling the kettle black?
That is the sort of arrogance that says "we know what is best".
Oh, oh!

The Hon. Member talks about dignity, Mr. Speaker. Let me talk to him about it. I would be glad to take him on a tour any time to talk to the thousands of people who lived in the core area of Winnipeg, people who had no jobs but who are now being trained and will get employment and have the dignity which work brings, all because of the expenditure of money by my Government. I would like to take the Member to the two or three thousand people who now hold housing units who did not have housing units before. He can tell them that they do not have dignity because of that investment. 1 would like the Hon. Member to talk to the students at the University of Manitoba who are now having an opportunity to be trained in new management studies and in new transportation research studies who are going on to new opportunities for jobs in a high technology world. The Member can tell them that they do not have dignity any more. I would like to take the Member and show him the opportunities for those kinds of investments that took place in a wide variety of neighbourhoods where people were able to start new businesses. I could take him to the warehouse district in Winnipeg where over 50 new businesses were started because of the core initiative. He can talk to the owners of those businesses and say, "You do not have dignity because the federal Liberal gave you an incentive grant to get your business started. We Tories would not do that. We would let you be without a business, without any ownership but with your dignity". That is basically what the Conservatives are talking about; they do not care about people. They do not care about a region like Manitoba. They
simply believe in their theology that the best way to do things is to do nothing at all.
I say to the Hon. Member that if he wants to learn how to start developing an economy, the best place for him to come to is Winnipeg. He will learn an awful lot more there than listening to anybody else in his Government.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) has indicated that our contracts and agreements are being ripped up along with the people in our cities and province. I would like that corrected because that is not the case. The Hon. Member implied that we as a Government are not honouring the commitments of the former Government with regard to agreements that were signed in the centre core area initiative-

-as well as with the former Minister of Transportation. These agreements to which the former Government committed itself are being honoured.

On the one hand the Member prides himself on the co-operation between the private entrepreneur, the free enterpriser, and his Government, but on the other hand he is firmly against the free enterprise system working with our Government to see that that National Research Council Centre is undertaken by private enterprise.
I sometimes find it difficult to understand the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry when he tries to imply that the contracts to which his Government had committed itself are not being honoured by this Government. They are. First, Mr. Speaker, I would say that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker) should get together with his colleague in front of him who said that all these things are so shameful and wasteful, that the Conservatives cannot stand it, but who now is saying, "We are very proud to go ahead and continue them". subtopic: TRUST COMPANIES-PIONEER TRUST COMPANY. (B) PROTECTION OF INVESTORS AND DEPOSITORS
TRUST COMPANIES-PIONEER TRUST COMPANY. (B) PROTECTION OF INVESTORS AND DEPOSITORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this point concerning questions which 1 directed to the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) on February 7, 1985. I asked the Minister to confirm whether Pioneer Trust of Regina, Saskatchewan, was in serious financial difficulties.

February 12, 1985
Adjournment Debate
In my supplementary question I asked her to guarantee that there would be a public inquiry or that at least the results of any internal inquiry would be made public. The Minister was good enough to give a decent answer. She said:
Mr. Speaker, I am sympathetic to the Hon. Member's question. I have already informed him that I will let him know of any further developments.
Further developments certainly occurred, in that two and a half hours later I was informed by the Minister's office that the Minister of Finance of the Province of Saskatchewan was at that moment making a public announcement, which in essence indicated that Pioneer Trust was closing its doors at four o'clock Regina time, that it would be placed in receivership, and that its assets would be taken over by Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation.
That evening I sent a letter by hand to the Minister, again making the request that a public inquiry be held into all matters pertaining to Pioneer Trust. I indicated that I believed it was in the public interest that there be an open inquiry into the reasons Pioneer Trust had to close its business and into the efforts that were made to keep it solvent. Also I indicated that depositors, shareholders in Pioneer Management Limited and the general public were entitled to a full accounting. I have requested on various occasions since then that a public inquiry be held, as there are many questions about Pioneer Trust which have been left unanswered.
Let me enumerate some of them. First, we are concerned whether the federal Government, particularly Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation, did everything possible to protect the interests of depositors. We feel that CDIC must have known of the problems which Pioneer had for most of 1984, if not before. Surely a cursory look at its financial statements over the last number of years would indicate that many of its assets were in real estate and that the value of those assets, particularly real estate assets in western Canada, particularly in British Columbia and Alberta, have declined in value.
Therefore, it is important to depositors in Pioneer Trust to know that the federal Government, through CDIC, did everything possible and reasonable to avert this disaster which has occurred and to make certain that Pioneer remained in a liquid and viable form and able to meet its obligations. That is one of the questions which I think a public inquiry should address. A public inquiry should look into the business practices of Pioneer Trust.
There is a great deal of uncertainty and many rumours floating around Regina and there is the feeling that perhaps improper loans were made and that a high enough interest rate was not charged on loans that were made. Did the company use sound business practices? Did it do the things it was supposed to do according to its charter of incorporation? These are all unanswered questions.
We would also like to know how much federal and provincial consultation occurred and when it occurred. Many of the events surrounding this past week seem to indicate that there
might have been a breakdown in communications. I believe that members of the Minister's staff were genuinely surprised when they learned on February 7 that the Saskatchewan Government had decided not to proceed with insuring the $30-million share issue that Pioneer Trust was going to market. We wonder what type of communication did occur between the federal and provincial Governments.
We are also concerned about the type of decisions that the Provincial Government has made. Before Christmas, the provincial Government announced that it would guarantee that $30-million share issue. That created a sense of optimism and trust. It now turns out that that was a false sense of optimism and trust. We are wondering whether or not the provincial Government knew what it was doing.
In summation, there are a great many questions that deserve to be answered in a full and public inquiry. We urge the Government to consider seriously establishing a public inquiry.

subtopic: TRUST COMPANIES-PIONEER TRUST COMPANY. (B) PROTECTION OF INVESTORS AND DEPOSITORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in response to the quite genuine concerns on the part of the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). I too have been concerned about this situation. I am happy to put on the record the steps that have been taken.
Senior management of Pioneer Trust Company made the decision to close the company's offices until further notice at the close of business on February 7, 1985. Management's decision came as a result of its inability to obtain support for a preferred share issue which Pioneer's shareholders had hoped to arrange. The proceeds of the preferred share issue would have been used in large part to replenish the capital base of the trust company. Given that this issue could not be successfully marketed, the continued operation of Pioneer no longer seemed viable and it therefore ceased operations.
On learning of management's decision and the proposed action, I in my capacity directed the federal Superintendent of Insurance to take control of Pioneer's assets so that the interests of the depositors would be best protected. Officers of the Department of Insurance were dispatched immediately to the company's offices and the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation was informed. An application to have the company wound up pursuant to the provisions of the Winding-up Act has been filed in the Court of Queen's Bench of Saskatchewan.
Pioneer Trust has approximately $243 million of deposits, of which about 90 per cent are fully insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. Officials of CDIC are now in Regina working on arrangements so that depositors may receive their funds to the extent of the $60,000 limit as quickly as possible once the winding-up order is issued. I am hopeful that by tomorrow there will be an announcement made outlining the arrangements that depositors can make.
Pioneer's current financial problems result mainly from the large proportion of its mortgage portfolio which is in arrears and from the necessity to write down the values of certain of its real estate investments, particularly those in areas which have experienced market depression. As a result of these
February 12, 1985

problems, the company experienced on the one hand a drain on its cash flow due to non-payment of mortgages and on the other a steady erosion of its capital base due to operating and capital losses. In the final analysis, the company became unable to meet the liquidity requirements imposed upon it by the Trust Companies Act and its borrowings exceeded those permitted by that statute.
On June 4, 1984, a hearing was held before the previous Minister of State for Finance which officials of the company attended. As a result of that hearing, limitations were placed on the company's licence with a view to restricting its investments to short-term high-quality debt securities, thereby bolstering its liquidity position and with a view to progressively reducing the company's borrowings by limitation of the interest rates offered by the company to depositors. The company's authorized borrowing multiple was also reduced, with the company being given until December 31, 1984 to comply.
The Hon. Member had two questions. One question dealt with the public inquiry, and I am satisfied that that is not necessary at this point. But I would like to reassure the House, with respect to other western trust companies, that I am not aware of any which are, as he has put it, on the brink of collapse.

Mr. Speaker, during the Question Period last Friday, I had hoped to pursue an important matter with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret). The matter dealt with the six issues which he is, by his own admission, currently discussing with Public Service staff associations.
All I wanted was some clarification, some precision, from the Minister as to whether in fact those six issues were: the master contract, political rights, a dental plan, adjustment procedures, amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act, and Public Service pensions.
Some clarification was and is certainly needed because, until the Minister mentioned the six issues in the House, no one else had, I had not, nor had the staff associations. As a matter of fact, the associations were stunned by the Minister's statement as they believed that the conversations they had with the Minister were in camera and, therefore, confidential.
Perhaps the Minister did not mean to mention the six issues. Perhaps they just popped into his head and on to the floor of the House when the Minister made a passing reference to the election promises which were made by his Party and by his Leader during the last election campaign.
The Minister's Leader and his Party made many promises during that campaign; in fact, hundreds of them. Fortunately, not all of them dealt with Public Service matters. In any case, my friend the Minister was not in the House last Friday and his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), under-
Adjournment Debate
took to answer in place of the President of the Treasury Board. The Minister of Finance either did not choose, or was not able to answer my question about which six issues precisely are being negotiated at this time. Instead, he told me how productive the discussions with the staff associations have been-at least that is the gospel according to the President of the Treasury Board-and how these discussions are expected to result in a great improvement in labour-management relations.
That is all very nice if it is true, but again the staff associations were somewhat mystified. They said last week that they had not yet had any hard input from the President of the Treasury Board on the positions which they had put forward to the Government for consideration. So it would seem to me that not only am I in the dark, and some of the participants in the Minister's discussions still in the dark, about the six issues that are under discussion, but so are the thousands of public servants in this country and the millions of Canadians who are most immediately concerned with the outcome of these negotiations.
I am hoping that this evening-

On Friday, Sir. I also asked, Mr. Speaker, because of the interesting progress which the President of the Treasury Board says he is making, because of the very productive discussions that he tells his colleagues he is having, when we can expect a signed agreement on all of these six issues. But

February 12, 1985
Adjournment Debate
no one was able or cared to tell me, or the House, what was happening. In fact, the Minister of Finance, on a vital, urgent matters, such as this, only told me that he did not think it was helpful for him or me, " ... to try to draw these discussions onto the floor of the House of Commons ..
I was surprised to hear that from the Minister of Finance. I know he qualified it slightly by referring to, and again I quote, " ... a point when they .. ."-talking about the negotiations- "... are at a sensitive stage and are clearly resulting in an improvement in the tone of labour-management relations". We are all in favour of that. But we only have the Minister's word about any improvement, Mr. Speaker. There has been no hard input from the President of the Treasury Board on the association's proposals. There is no agreement signed. There is nothing to prove the Minister's statement. As far as "drawing" the discussions on to the floor of the House of Commons is concerned, it seems to me that that is a much more appropriate place than in the corridors of the House, which is where the President of the Treasury Board took them. It is far more legitimate, as far as 1 am concerned, to have the details given on the floor of the House, to Members of Parliament, than given to the media outside the House as was done last week.
My purpose, Mr. Speaker, has never been in any way to interfere with any discussions that might be under way or in any way to prejudice them, either on the floor of the House or anywhere else. My purpose has only been to obtain answers to questions which I have raised here in this House. They were legitimate questions, seriously asked. I hope that someone on the government side will be able to give me some answers.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that I am still waiting for an answer to a question I raised on February 4 which was specifically: when new contracts are negotiated with the Public Service Alliance or with Public Service unions in general, will job classification be made negotiable? The President of the Treasury Board answered that progress was to be expected and that, indeed, he was very happy with the progress being made on the six issues. I raise this question with the Parliamentary Secretary: where are we at this time?
