The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) said in the House on February 4, in response to a question raised by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), that he had had a number of meetings over the past few months with the Public Service union leaders and that progress was being made on the package of issues under discussion. Outside the House later that day, in response to reporters' questions, he reiterated that discussion to date had gone along quite well and added that he hoped to have an agreement on the package in a very short time.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier seek to disrupt any negotiations which the Government might be having with the union.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT-JOB CLASSIFICATIONS. (B) AGREEMENT INQUIRY
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT-JOB CLASSIFICATIONS. (B) AGREEMENT INQUIRY
speechtext:
We are not about to let that happen, Mr. Speaker. It is unfortunate that the President's remarks have been interpreted in some quarters as an indication that the Government is near or has reached an agreement with the unions. Further discussions are required with the unions before the President of the Treasury Board is in a position to ask his colleagues to approve a course of action for the reasonable disposition of the issues. Unfortunately, the President had to cancel his last scheduled meeting with the unions on rather short notice but it is his firm intention to resume discussions with them at an early date with a view to having decisions taken on the issues within the time frame he has outlined to them in discussions.
When the parties last met, there was tacit agreement that while talks continued, they would refrain from staking out their positions publicly and would confine themselves to stating that there are a number of issues and solutions and that discussions are taking place on them. In contrast to the way the previous administration dealt with unions, we keep our word. It is evident, Mr. Speaker, from the discussions which have taken place that the union leaders share this Government's desire to improve union management relations in the Public Service. This is in direct contrast to the way relations deteriorated under the former Liberal Government.
I will not frustrate their desires, nor will I break the Party's confidences and jeopardize a mutually satisfactory outcome of the discussions. I wish to assure the Hon. Member, however, that the President of the Treasury Board intends to resume discussions with the unions on the issues at the earliest possible date and remains confident that an early agreement can be reached.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday, during Question Period, the Minister of State for Transport (Mr. Bouchard) made the absurd and incorrect statement that the responsibility of replying to my question on car pollution controls rested with the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier). The Department of Transport, as the Minister well knows, is the only Department responsible for introducing automobile emission controls. I do not know whether to ask myself whether the Minister of State for Transport (Mr. Bouchard) really knows what his Department is responsible for, or whether we should all view this incident as another example of a Government that does not know what it is doing. But one thing is obvious. We have two Ministers of Transport who share two different views on what their Department should be doing. One shirks his responsibility by shifting the onus of responsibility to the Minister of the Environment. The other, the senior Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankow-ski), recognizes that automobile emission controls is a matter for which his Department has the responsibility, but he procrastinates. He would rather not decide. Meanwhile, we have a Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who talks a good fight about the need for a cleaner environment. He wants to go to Quebec City next month for his meeting with President Reagan with
February 12, 1985

"clean hands". But the Prime Minister should know that if he wants to be squeaky clean for the President of the United States, he should talk to his Ministers of Transport about announcing automobile emission controls very soon.
Of course, if he is really in a talkative mood, Mr. Speaker, he might remind the Minister of the Environment that she should also be concerned about automobile emission controls, because so far she has not demonstrated a great environmental concern. Of course, the Prime Minister may just have to face up to reality and come to grips with the fact that he has a Department of Transport headed by two Ministers, who either do not understand the importance of the meeting with President Reagan or who just do not care if an accord is reached on finding a joint solution to our common problem of acid rain.
The Prime Minister must decide which way he is going to lean. If he supports the Minister of Transport, who seems reluctant to make a decision on emission controls, he faces the problem of disregarding his own environmental problems. Let us hope the Prime Minister will be able to overcome the reticence of his recalcitrant Minister of Transport.
The battle on this important issue, Mr. Speaker, will take place behind the closed doors of Cabinet. Most likely it will centre on when rather than whether the new regulations will become effective. Who will win? Will it be the Prime Minister, so his hands will be clean for President Reagan? Will it be the Minister of Transport, who wants to take more time before he takes action? Or will it be the Minister of the Environment, who so far has indicated she is more concerned with industry than the environment? Let us hope, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister will emerge as the winner. The bottom line question is, when will the car emission controls become effective? Will it be 1987, 1988, 1989 or 1990, or will it be later? From an environmental as well an economic point of view, the obvious answer is 1987.

speechtext:
There were a lot of rhetorical questions being asked by the Hon. Member when the fact of the matter was that he was the Minister of the Environment and watched all the delay and procrastination on the part of the previous Liberal Government. That is a shame, and the Hon. Member should know better than to bring it up.
I want the Hon. Member to know that for more than two years officials of the Departments of Transport, Environment, Health and Welfare, Energy, Mines and Resources, and Regional Industrial Expansion have been studying the effects of motor vehicle exhaust emission on the health of Canadians and on the environment through the formation of acid rain. That is probably the first time the Hon. Member ever heard that. These studies have also considered the potential impact of possible regulatory changes on the petroleum and automotive industries as well as on consumers. I want to tell the Hon. Member that there have been a large number of reports, all prepared under the previous administration. But the previous administration did nothing. I want the Hon. Member to know that in less than six months since we have been in office we have been able to arrange public hearings where all interested Parties could table data and express views. In addition, the present Government has managed the completion of all the analytical work. In contrast to the complete inaction when the Hon. Member was the Minister, the results are in and are presently being reviewed by the Ministers of Transport, the Environment, Health, Energy and Industry. I can assure the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) that in contrast to the years of inaction by the Liberal Party, there will be an appropriate announcement very shortly.
